articles.title: A Critical Epistemological Audit of Early Evidence Syntheses in Generative AI Educational Research: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
articles.authors: Tim Fütterer; Nina Peltzer; Peter Gerjets; Detmar Meurers; Tamara Powell Tate; Mark Warschauer; Valentin Emslander; Lisa Bardach; John hattie; Michael Sailer
articles.abstract: The rapid emergence of ChatGPT in education was accompanied by an equally rapid proliferation of meta-analyses synthesizing its effects on educational outcomes. We conducted a systematic epistemological audit of the first wave of these meta-analyses, evaluating both their methodological and reporting quality and the primary evidence they synthesized. We included meta-analyses published after the release of ChatGPT that quantitatively synthesized its effects on educational outcomes. Five meta-analyses comprising 87 unique primary studies met our inclusion criteria. We also reconstructed their quantitative evidence base and conducted exploratory three-level random-effects meta-analyses to examine effect magnitude, heterogeneity, and robustness, and how these varied with theoretically and methodologically relevant characteristics. The five meta-analyses generally searched multiple databases, specified eligibility criteria, and examined heterogeneity and potential publication bias, but showed limitations in independent screening and coding, preregistration, open data and code, and transparent reporting. The underlying primary evidence likewise showed methodological and reporting limitations and substantial conceptual heterogeneity. Among 69 classifiable primary studies, 79.7% assessed performance exclusively, whereas only 11.6% assessed learning exclusively. The reconstructed meta-analysis yielded a positive average effect (g = 0.83, 95% CI [0.68, 0.97]), but heterogeneity was substantial (I² = 94.06%; 95% prediction interval [−0.75, 2.41]), and estimates were markedly attenuated in sensitivity analyses addressing small-study and selection effects. Although positive effects remained among stronger studies assessing learning, increasingly stringent quality criteria rapidly reduced the evidence base, limiting the certainty and generalizability of conclusions about learning effects. Overall, our findings caution against interpreting a single pooled estimate as a stable general effect of ChatGPT on learning and highlight the need for more rigorous, conceptually precise, transparent, and reproducible research.

articles.title: Configural Object Novelty Alters Network Coordination Across the Medial Temporal Lobe
articles.authors: Lauren Alexandra Homann; Jennifer D. Ryan; Rosanna K. Olsen; Natalia Ladyka-Wojcik; Morgan Barense
articles.abstract: Object identity depends on how constituent features are combined, such that the same features may form distinct objects when their configuration changes. The perirhinal (PRC) and anterolateral entorhinal (alERC) cortices are implicated in such conjunctive object processing; however, regional sensitivity alone cannot reveal how information is coordinated across regions, or whether this coordination extends beyond object-processing regions to spatial and relational regions. Using generalized psychophysiological interaction (gPPI) analysis of BOLD signals extracted from manually-segmented medial temporal lobe regions, we examined task-modulated functional connectivity while younger adults viewed repeated objects (familiar features in familiar configurations), recombined objects (familiar features in novel configurations), and novel objects (novel features in novel configurations). This design permitted isolation of connectivity changes associated with configural, featural, and global object novelty. Configural novelty (repeated vs. recombined objects) was associated with widespread reductions in connectivity spanning anterior-temporal, posterior-medial, and hippocampal regions, extending to medial prefrontal and posterior-medial cortex, alongside more limited increases in connectivity between posteromedial entorhinal cortex (pmERC) and superior parietal and frontal regions. In contrast, featural novelty (recombined vs. novel objects) and global novelty (repeated vs. novel objects) were not associated with significant connectivity differences. These findings demonstrate that configural object novelty alters coordination across a distributed hippocampal-cortical network, with connectivity effects extending beyond the anterior-temporal regions traditionally implicated in object processing, highlighting how object and relational processing systems work in concert to support conjunctive object processing. Connectivity thus provides a complementary window onto how conjunctive information is coordinated, beyond what regional sensitivity alone can reveal.

articles.title: LLM-Generated Well-being Intervention Recommendations Are Sensitive to Psychological Profiles: A Proof-of-Concept Expert-Rating Study
articles.authors: Benjamin Kaveladze; Elizabeth Webb Lampe; Michael V. Heinz; Lisa Marsch; Andrew T. Campbell; Nicholas C. Jacobson
articles.abstract: Personalizing digital well-being interventions to fit the needs and preferences of individual users has been a longstanding challenge. Large language models (LLMs) may be well-suited for this task, using natural language reasoning to integrate heterogeneous user information into personalized guidance. We tested whether LLMs could generate intervention recommendations that were sensitive to differences across recipients’ psychological profiles. Across 178 undergraduate student profiles spanning 14 psychological measures, four LLMs recommended 10 scripted chatbot dialogues from a library of 222 options. Next, two experts rated the recommendations’ appropriateness for a given profile (1-10). For half of the profiles, raters saw recommendations generated for that student (matched condition); for the remainder, they saw recommendations generated for a different student (unmatched condition). As hypothesized, matched recommendations (M = 6.74) were rated as more appropriate than unmatched ones (M = 5.64, SMD = 0.50). These results provide evidence that LLMs can adapt their intervention recommendations to match psychological profiles. However, inter-rater reliability was poor (ICC = 0.22), and all LLMs showed substantial sensitivity to catalog order. As such, we stress the preliminary nature of the findings. Whether such tailoring translates into improved well-being outcomes for users remains to be tested.

articles.title: Inter-lexical inhibition is present early and has a unique developmental trajectory: evidence from a novel version of sub-phonemic mismatch
articles.authors: John Baltazar Muegge; Keith Baxelbaum; Abigail Fergus; Bob McMurray
articles.abstract: Lateral inhibition is a key property of spoken word recognition and has been implicated as an important factor in novel word learning and a locus of difference for some language disorders. Work on the development of lateral inhibition has produced mixed results, however, suggesting that it may not be fully operative in young children and has a protracted developmental trajectory. Here, we posit that these results have less to do with a lack of inhibition at these ages and is more a product of limitations of the common paradigm used to index inhibition, the sub-phonemic mismatch task. We introduce a variant of sub-phonemic mismatch which is able to detect inhibition at these early age groups. 236 children from grades 2-5 were given a multisyllabic word (battleship) whose initial portion could contain acoustic cues towards a nonword (bettle-ship) or another lexical item (bottle-ship). Eye-movements made across these conditions revealed that children have robust lateral inhibition even at young ages. Importantly, the strength of this inhibition is largely stable across ages. Further exploratory analyses suggest that development does occur, but in the timing or duration of inhibition instead of its magnitude. A follow-up experiment with adults replicates and clarifies this finding, suggesting a novel framework for understanding inhibition.

articles.title: What You Miss Won’t Move You: Awareness Connects Respiratory Change to Subjective Arousal
articles.authors: Norman A. S. Farb; Kyle Logie; Rose Amir Pour
articles.abstract: Does physiological arousal shape emotion only when consciously perceived? Existing paradigms confound detection with signal magnitude, rendering this question intractable. The Breath Change Awareness Task (BCAT) resolves this confound by orthogonally manipulating signal magnitude and detection. Across five studies of undergraduate and community samples (total N = 787), detected changes produced arousal scaled to magnitude; equivalent undetected changes produced no differential response. In a pre-registered laboratory study with physiological verification (Study 5; N = 206), belt recordings confirmed physical compliance, and arousal gating was stronger during interoceptive engagement than visual tracking. Self-reported interoceptive awareness (MAIA) predicted detection confidence but not objective threshold, reflecting a disposition toward bodily awareness rather than detection ability. Conscious detection gates interoceptive arousal transfer: physiological change moves us only when we notice it. Findings are based on self-reported arousal and predominantly undergraduate samples, and warrant replication with clinical populations and objective physiological measures.

articles.title: Identity in Tune?  School Identity Development Predicts Declining Preferences for Non-Mainstream Music Preferences Across Adolescence
articles.authors: Andrik Becht; Tom ter Bogt
articles.abstract: This pre-registered study examined within-person longitudinal associations between adolescents’ school identity and preferences for non-mainstream music. Media Delinquency Theory proposes that weaker school identity precedes stronger non-mainstream music preferences, whereas Music Marker Theory proposes reverse effects. Random-intercept cross-lagged panel models were estimated among 900 adolescents (M age at T1 = 12.38 years, 50.1% female). Results provided limited support for Media Delinquency Theory: weaker school identity commitment predicted stronger preferences for heavy metal, whereas music preferences did not predict changes in school identity. Increasing reconsideration of school identity predicted lower preferences for heavy metal and goth music in middle adolescence. At the between-person level, weaker school identity commitment was associated with stronger goth preferences. Adolescents’ attraction to non-mainstream music became increasingly stable during adolescence.

articles.title: What Kind of Disliked Group Are Environmentalists? A Four-Sample Test of the Dual-Process Model
articles.authors: Taciano L Milfont; Felipe Vilanova; Angelo Brandelli Costa
articles.abstract: Right-Wing Authoritarianism (RWA) and Social Dominance Orientation (SDO) are well-established correlates of weaker environmentalism but less is known about how these ideologies relate to attitudes toward environmentalists as a social group. Drawing on the Dual-Process Motivational model, this brief research report first examines whether environmentalists are disliked as a dangerous, derogated or dissident group, using secondary analyses of four Brazilian samples (Ntotal = 1,679; Mage = 39.12 years, SDage = 15.34; 53.9% women). Social perceptions of environmentalists were positive on average, and attitudes toward environmentalists correlated most strongly with prejudice toward dissident groups (pooled r = .52). Confirmatory factor models confirmed that environmentalists loaded most strongly on the dissident factor in every sample (λs = .38 to .74), with smaller derogated loadings in two samples and null or negative dangerous loadings. We then examined how these ideologies relate to prejudiced attitudes toward environmentalists. RWA and SDO showed independent positive associations overall (pooled βs = .23 and .28), and their coefficients did not differ significantly in any sample after adjustment for multiple comparisons. Negativity toward environmentalists thus aligns with prejudice toward groups seen as challenging the status quo and is associated with both authoritarian and dominance-related ideology.

articles.title: Positive and Self-Transcendent Eco-Emotions as Fuel for Collective Action: A Social Identity Account
articles.authors: Ronan Bellemin; Anna Tcherkassof; Aurélien GRATON
articles.abstract: Emotions are key predictors of pro-environmental behavior. Despite the growing interest in eco-emotions in recent years, negative eco-emotions can be detrimental, which opens the way for the study of positive and self-transcendent eco-emotions. Across four pre-registered studies, we examined how positive and self-transcendent eco-emotions relate to pro environmental collective action through group-based processes. A correlational study (N = 502) revealed that positive and self-transcendent eco-emotions were associated with pro environmental collective action intentions, mediated by pro-environmental ingroup identification. An online experiment (N = 387) inducing eco-compassion found neither significant effect on actual donations nor mediation by ingroup identification. A replication of the first study (N = 461) confirmed the mediation effect on intentions. Finally, an online experiment inducing awe at nature (N = 542) demonstrated that this emotion increased pro environmental collective action intentions, again mediated by pro-environmental ingroup identification. Together, these findings support social identity frameworks in which affective reactions act as motivational levers for collective engagement.

articles.title: When the brain can change: effects of neuroplasticity education on beliefs about brain-based mental disorders
articles.authors: Olha Guley; Elena Pasquinelli; Daniel Nettle
articles.abstract: Mental disorders are increasingly framed as brain-based, which can promote pessimism about recovery. We tested whether brief education about neuroplasticity, the brain’s capacity to change throughout life, can counter these beliefs. Across three preregistered vignette experiments with UK adults (Ns = 414, 411, and 418), participants viewed a brain-framed mental disorder after either a brief neuroplasticity video and text intervention or a matched control. The intervention increased the perceived possibility of recovery, but this effect was short-lived after a single exposure in Study 1 and more durable with a booster in Study 2. The effect in Study 3 was not significant, but a pooled analysis of data from Studies 2 and 3 confirmed the positive effect overall. The intervention did not affect perceived treatment efficacy, nor did it reduce desired social distance from people with mental disorders. In Study 3, higher familiarity with the disorder was associated with a higher perceived recovery and lower desired social distance. These findings suggest neuroplasticity education can increase public optimism about recovery from mental disorders, but changing treatment beliefs or social attitudes may require more targeted interventions.

articles.title: Cognitive impairment in older adults with type 1 diabetes: Influence of premorbid ability and associations with depression, anxiety, and diabetes-related distress
articles.authors: Lily Li; Dana Wong; Caroline Fisher; Jennifer Conn; Spiros Fourlanos; Paul Wraight; Kerryn Elizabeth Pike
articles.abstract:
Objective: This study characterised cognitive and psychological functioning in older adults with type 1 diabetes (T1D), compared the prevalence of cognitive impairment under age-based and premorbid-ability+age-adjusted (PA+AA) norms, and examined associations between cognitive status and depression, anxiety, and diabetes-related distress.

Method: Forty-three adults aged ≥55 years with T1D completed a comprehensive neuropsychological assessment covering attention, working memory, verbal and visuospatial memory, processing speed, executive function, verbal fluency, and confrontation naming, alongside measures of depression (PHQ-9), anxiety (GAD-7), and diabetes-related distress (PAID-11). Impairment was defined as performance ≥1.5 SD below expected levels on at least two tests, with expected scores derived from either age-based norms or estimated premorbid ability combined with age.

Results: Group-level performance was within or above age-expected ranges. Individually, 14% met criteria for impairment under age-based norms versus 42% under PA+AA norms; the additional 28% were identified only against estimated prior ability. Impairments were most frequent in confrontation naming and processing speed. PA+AA norms additionally revealed impairments in attention, working memory, verbal fluency, and cognitive flexibility. Impaired participants reported significantly higher depression under both approaches. Anxiety was significantly elevated under PA+AA norms, and diabetes-related distress under age-based norms only.

Conclusions: Age-based norms may substantially underestimate cognitive impairment in older adults with T1D, particularly among those with higher premorbid ability. The association between impairment and elevated psychological distress supports the integration of cognitive and mood assessment in routine diabetes care.

articles.title: The Vanderbilt Report’s critique of humanistic scholarship is itself bad scholarship and should be corrected or retracted
articles.authors: Patrick E. Savage
articles.abstract: Vanderbilt University’s “Report on the State of Scholarship in the Humanities and the Humanistic Social Sciences” (Boghossian et al., June 25, 2026) argued that humanistic scholarship has experienced “a deterioration in scholarly standards fueled by the substitution of political criteria for properly scholarly criteria”. The initial (August 2026) version of my critique emphasised that these conclusions were primarily based on unpublished, unverifiable data. Now that most of the data underlying the report (largely from unvalidated Large Language Model [LLM] categorisations) have been belatedly published, I show that these data do not support the report’s main claims. I briefly review the main data from each published disciplinary sub-report (music studies, anthropology, sociology, history, literary studies). Overall, there is an utterly indefensible mismatch between the actual empirical data (e.g., decreases in the ratio of Western classical music vs. all other music studied) and Boghossian et al.’s conclusions of an overall “deterioration in scholarly standards”. While I agree with the authors that critical evaluation of the quality of academic scholarship is urgently needed in today’s global political climate, the report’s main conclusions are not remotely justified by their data and are likely to hinder rather than facilitate informed debate. I recommend Boghossian et al.’s report be corrected or retracted to resolve these issues.

articles.title: Everyday Encounters with Economic Inequality
articles.authors: Carla Moccia; Matthew John Easterbrook; Matthias S Gobel
articles.abstract: Research on economic inequality has traditionally relied on macro-level indices, though a growing body of work examines how economic inequality is perceived in everyday life. Whether different forms of everyday encounters carry different political and psychological consequences remains unclear. Across four studies with London-based samples (N = 1,554), we used a situation-sampling approach to identify forms of real-world inequality encounters and test how they relate to appraisal, redistribution support, and psychological distress. Study 1 identified two forms of inequality: Structural Inequality, describing disparities in essential goods and institutions, and Lifestyle Inequality, involving differences in consumption, leisure, and social participation. Study 2 showed that Structural situations were perceived as more unequal and unfair and elicited stronger redistribution support than Lifestyle Inequality situations. Study 3a, reported in Supplementary Materials, showed that greater redistribution support for Structural Inequality situations was largely carried through greater perceived unfairness. Study 3b modelled Structural and Lifestyle Inequality content continuously: Structural Inequality was linked to redistribution support and distress through unfairness, whereas Lifestyle Inequality was linked to distress through upward social comparison. The political and psychological consequences of inequality therefore depend on the form of encounter, not only on its perceived magnitude.

articles.title: Digital Stress: Theoretical Conceptualizations, Empirical Findings, and Tasks for Future Research
articles.authors: Leonard Reinecke; Frank M. Schneider; Alicia Gilbert
articles.abstract: Over the past decade, mobile Internet-enabled digital devices have provided ubiquitous access to media content and communication, resulting in unprecedented levels of “always on” media use. As a consequence, many users feel stressed and strained by the new demands of digital media use. A fast-growing field of research has addressed such forms of “digital stress” and its psychological implications. The present chapter provides a review and theoretical integration of the state of digital stress research. After an introduction to the basic psychological mechanisms underlying stress reactions based on the Transactional Model of Stress (Lazarus & Folkman, 1984), the chapter reviews and synthesizes existing definitions of digital stress. It then summarizes and systematizes key empirical findings regarding the central predictors, boundary conditions, and effects of digital stress. The review concludes with a discussion of recent developments, open questions, and future challenges for the field of digital stress research.

articles.title: The Influence of Victim Gender and Professional Identity on Perceptions of AI-Generated Image Abuse
articles.authors: Matthew Richard Ivory; Sophie J Nightingale
articles.abstract: Artificially-Generated Non-Consensual Intimate Imagery (AI-NCII) is a form of gender-based violence and sexual abuse. Modern AI tools enable the easy creation of highly realistic NCII, with the potential to cause very real and profound harms to those depicted. Although victim characteristics, such as gender and sexual activity, are known to influence third-party judgements, less is understood about how victims from stigmatised or marginalised groups are judged and how these characteristics influence victim blame and perceptions of harm. In this preregistered vignette study, participants were presented with a hypothetical scenario describing a transgender or cisgender sex worker or office worker who was the victim of AI-NCII creation and subsequent sharing. The ideal victim framework and expectancy violations theory were used to interpret who was blamed and perceived as harmed, and why. Results revealed that sex workers were blamed more and perceived as less harmed than office workers. It was also observed that while transgender victims were blamed more by men than women, they were perceived as experiencing comparable levels of harm to cisgender victims. The findings suggest when victims do not conform to expected norms or are perceived to engage in behaviours inconsistent with ideal victim expectations, public sympathy may be reduced. Future interventions should therefore prioritise education about victimisation and challenge the expectations and beliefs that shape judgements of victims, rather than place responsibility on victims to conform to an ideal or reduce the visibility of their identities.

articles.title: Differences in AI Anxiety: Exploratory Factor Analysis Suggests Similar AI Anxiety Structure in German- and English-Speaking Samples
articles.authors: Nick Sheth; Klemens Weigl
articles.abstract: The mass use of AI applications is transforming human-AI interaction while uncovering and intensifying AI anxieties. To measure these anxieties in German-speaking populations, this study translates and psychometrically evaluates the Artificial Intelligence Anxiety Scale (AIAS) [31]. In contrast to a concurrently German published version by Hajek et al. [9] exploratory factor analysis (EFA) is employed to test whether a distinct anxiety structure emerges from the data. A quota sample (N = 225) with balanced age and gender representation completed an online survey. The full scale (α = .95) and subscales (α = .85-.96) demonstrated good to excellent reliability. EFA identified four factors: learning, AI configuration, replacement, and socio-technical blindness, largely consistent with the original English structure. Five items required removal, suggesting cultural and linguistic specificity. Limitations include the sample’s composition and the factor characteristics. The German AIAS provides a reliable instrument for human-AI interaction research and targeted anxiety interventions.

articles.title: A general method for estimating reliability using Bayesian Measurement Uncertainty
articles.authors: Giacomo Bignardi; Rogier Kievit; Paul - Christian Bürkner
articles.abstract: Unreliable measurement can lead to lower statistical power, attenuated effect sizes and residual confounding. However, estimating reliability can be challenging for complex cognitive and behavioural assessments without test-retest data. Most statistical methods for assessing reliability with a single test administration are designed for fixed-item questionnaires. We introduce a novel Bayesian procedure called relative measurement uncertainty (RMU) for estimating reliability that can be broadly applied, including to many widely used computational models. Our approach draws pairs of samples from each subject's posterior and calculates the correlation between draws. We demonstrate analytically and via simulation that this method provides accurate reliability estimates and well-calibrated credible intervals across linear factor, signal detection and reinforcement learning models. Simulations found that RMU was more accurate (lower root mean square error) than existing measures (coefficient alpha, coefficient H, split-half), but more importantly, it can be applied across a wide range of computational models. RMU offers a general method for estimating reliability, leveraging the modelling flexibility of Bayesian statistical methods.

articles.title: A Two-Stage Scaffolding Model of Color and Luminance Development: Retinal Waves, Global Impoverishment, and Luminance-Grounded Object Representations
articles.authors: David Henry Peterzell
articles.abstract: How does the visual system construct object representations that are robust to the removal of color? I propose a two-stage scaffolding model. In Stage 1 (prenatal), retinal waves establish spectrally non-selective spatiotemporal contrast sensitivity, the necessary structural foundation of the visual system, before any visual experience occurs. Because the wave-generating circuitry encodes only contrasts in firing rate with no access to spectral information, this foundation is necessarily achromatic: whatever circuits retinal waves entrain, they are trained on a signal that carries no chromatic content. In Stage 2 (postnatal), the globally degraded neonatal visual signal, low spatial resolution, low contrast sensitivity, and immature chromatic processing, all coupled through shared photoreceptor immaturity, forces the first object representations to be built on luminance structure, the only dimension with sufficient fidelity under maximal front-end degradation. Together, these two stages explain why normal observers recognize objects in grayscale as readily as in color: luminance structure was the foundation of object representations from the beginning. The model also explains why late-sighted individuals who gain sight after dense congenital cataracts show disproportionate reliance on color: they retain the prenatal structural scaffold (intact retinas generating normal retinal waves) but lack the postnatal experiential scaffold (years of globally impoverished visual experience that normally grounds object representations in luminance). The model generates testable predictions that distinguish it from color-specific developmental accounts, and several can be evaluated on existing computational architectures without new patient data.

articles.title: Fleeting Attention While Scrolling: Dwell Time and Exposure in Social Media Feeds
articles.authors: Douglas A. Parry; Philipp K. Masur
articles.abstract: Social media feeds expose users to rapidly changing streams of content, but relatively little is known about how long individual posts remain available for processing during user-controlled scrolling. We analyzed high-resolution behavioural logs from a fully interactive, simulated Instagram-like platform, to characterize dwell time and identify factors associated with variation in exposure duration. Preregistered analyses included 43,921 post-viewing episodes from 1,102 participants. Exposure was typically brief and highly variable, with the median dwell time lasting only 0.93 seconds. Mixed-effects models showed little evidence that visual complexity, valence, arousal, thematic content, presence of a face, social reinforcement, or measured individual characteristics were associated with dwell time. Instead, dwell time declined substantially across the browsing sequence and was considerably longer for posts encountered on profile and explore pages than in the main feed. These findings characterize social media browsing as a sequence of heterogeneous, often momentary exposures and demonstrate the value of simulated platforms for studying scrolling behavior at high temporal resolution.

articles.title: Scroll and Snack: Daily Life Exposure to Healthy Food Content on Instagram Boosts Cravings for Healthy Snacks
articles.authors: Monique Caroline Alblas; Matthias Burkard Aulbach; Lena Jeremias; Veronika Pavlovova; Leonardo Pimpini
articles.abstract: Background: Food content pervades social media, yet how everyday exposure shapes momentary craving and snacking in daily life remains unclear. We tested whether experimentally adding unhealthy (H1) vs. healthy (H2) food content on top of participants’ Instagram feeds increased craving for and intake of unhealthy and healthy snacks, relative to adding art content (control). Method: In this preregistered randomized controlled field trial, 116 healthy-weight young adults (Mage = 22.46 years, 79.3% female) completed a 10-day smartphone ecological momentary assessment protocol (five prompts/day; five baseline, five manipulation days). Participants were randomly assigned to follow existing preselected Instagram accounts featuring unhealthy food, healthy food, or art (control); the number of additional accounts was 5% of those already followed. Outcomes (craving, consumption) were modeled using multilevel linear mixed models. Results: Manipulation checks confirmed expected shifts in food-related Instagram content. Against H1, added unhealthy content increased neither craving for (p = .194) nor intake of (p = .867) unhealthy snacks. Supporting H2, healthy food content increased craving for healthy snacks relative to both the control and the unhealthy condition (p < .001), but not healthy snack intake (p = .061). Conclusions: Curating a healthier Instagram feed may increase the desire for healthy snacks, but this effect, possibly due to the short duration of the manipulation, did not extend to intentions and/or intake. In conclusion, food craving may thus be used as early intervention target in future weight loss intervention, whereas changing actual intake likely requires longer or personalized exposure.

articles.title: Preliminary Effects of PRECISE, a Personalized and Idiographically-Tailored Adjunctive Intervention for Treating Suicidal Ideation and Psychiatric Symptoms in Young Adults: Open Trial
articles.authors: Kevin Scott Kuehn; Raeanne C. Moore; Katherine T. Foster; Colin A. Depp
articles.abstract:
Background: Individuals at high risk for suicide are phenomenologically heterogeneous, yet most evidence-based interventions deliver the same content to everyone. Dialectical behavior therapy (DBT) is effective but lengthy, in part because every patient receives the full skills curriculum regardless of which skills address their own drivers of risk. PeRsonalizEd Clinical Intervention for Suicidal Events (PRECISE) uses idiographic models derived from each participant’s ecological momentary assessment (EMA) data to identify and teach only the DBT skills most relevant to that individual, allowing treatment to be delivered in six weeks.

Objective: This study aimed to evaluate the feasibility, acceptability, and preliminary impact of PRECISE on suicidal thoughts and behaviors (STBs), depressive and anxiety symptoms, and related secondary outcomes.

Methods: Thirty young adults (ages 18–26) with active STBs, recruited from a university and the surrounding community, enrolled in a six-week course of PRECISE alongside five times per day EMA in a single-arm open trial. STBs were assessed at baseline, 6 weeks, and 12 weeks using the Columbia-Suicide Severity Rating Scale (CSSRS) and the Modified Scale for Suicidal Ideation (MSSI); depressive and anxiety symptoms (PROMIS), coping self-efficacy (CSES), and emotion regulation strategy use (CERQ) were also assessed. Bayesian multilevel models with participant-level random intercepts estimated change over time.

Results: Retention was 93% (28/30) at 6 weeks and 87% (26/30) at 12 weeks. Participants attended a mean of 5.4 of 6 coaching sessions and rated the intervention as highly acceptable (AIM: M = 17.2), appropriate (IAM: M = 16.9), and feasible (FIM: M = 17.2; each out of 20). From baseline to 12 weeks, suicidal ideation declined on both measures (CSSRS: −2.28 points, 95% CrI [−2.75, −1.81]; MSSI: −5.38 points, 95% CrI [−8.21, −2.53]; probability of direction [pd] ≥ 99.99%). Depressive symptoms (−6.51 T-score points, 95% CrI [−8.60, −4.38]) and anxiety symptoms (−3.60, 95% CrI [−5.70, −1.50]) also declined, and coping self-efficacy increased (+29.30 points, 95% CrI [18.21, 40.50]; all pd ≥ 99.95%). Maladaptive emotion regulation strategy use showed a smaller, less certain decline (−3.20 points, 95% CrI [−6.42, 0.03]; pd = 97.36%), and adaptive strategy use showed no credible change (0.97 points, 95% CrI [−3.75, 5.63]). No serious adverse events or suicide attempts occurred; 11 mild episodes of non-suicidal self-injury were reported by 5 participants.

Conclusions: In this open trial, a brief intervention that personalizes DBT skills using participants' own idiographic EMA data was feasible, acceptable, and associated with clinically meaningful and sustained reductions in STBs, psychiatric symptoms, and maladaptive coping skills as well as improvements in coping self-efficacy. Pending further confirmatory testing, PRECISE may be a useful suicide prevention approach.

articles.title: Rumination under the microscope: causal discovery and inference of the effect of rumination on depressive symptoms in an N-of-1 time series
articles.authors: Pedro Henrique Ribeiro Santiago; Alyssa Sawyer; Mark Kohler; Lisa Jamieson; Carly Sutherland
articles.abstract: Depression is one of the most prevalent and disabling mental health conditions worldwide, with an estimated 5.7% of adults currently experiencing depression, around 332 million people globally. Rumination, a repetitive pattern of thinking that involves comparing one’s circumstances with how one would ideally like them to be without engaging in problem-solving, is the cognitive vulnerability most strongly associated with depression. Despite the evidence, there are no studies that have employed causal discovery and inference to investigate whether rumination has a causal effect on depressive mood using N-of-1 psychological time series data. To address this gap, this study conducted a secondary analysis of publicly available data on an American Latino Female diagnosed with Major Depressive Disorder (MDD) who reported on her feelings 4 times per day over 39 days. To conduct causal discovery, the Vector Autoregressive Linear Non-Gaussian Acyclic Model (VAR-LiNGAM) algorithm was used. To conduct causal inference, the g-formula, implemented via a Monte Carlo simulation, was used to estimate the Contemporaneous Effect, the 1-lag Structural Direct Effect and the 1-lag Total Effect of rumination on depressed mood. The findings indicated that high rumination was associated with a 15.6-point increase in depressed mood contemporaneously and a 1.7-point increase in depressed mood approximately 4 hours later. This evidence further substantiates the importance of interventions designed to reduce ruminative thinking and, consequently, improve depressive symptoms.

articles.title: Feeling the heat: How climate emotions shape trust in government and policy support across 68 countries
articles.authors: Jlenia Avellino; Fabienne Stucki; Omid Ghasemi; Viktoria Cologna; Theofilos Gkinopoulos; Niels G. Mede; Stylianos Syropoulos; Sebastian Berger
articles.abstract: Negative emotions related to climate change can adversely impact people’s mental health and wellbeing. However, they could also accelerate action on climate change by driving support for environmental policies. Using the TISP Many Labs data, we present results from a cross-sectional secondary analysis of survey responses from 69,534 participants across 68 countries worldwide. The survey included items on people’s emotional response to climate change, perceptions of government responses to climate change, and support for environmental policies. Participants experienced relatively low levels of negative emotions toward climate change (M = 2.79, SD = 1.01; 1 = not at all, 5 = very strongly), with relatively little variation across countries (SD = 0.27). Individuals reporting stronger negative emotions were less satisfied with their government’s climate action and expressed greater support for environmental policies. Our results thereby contribute to a global assessment of climate emotions and its correlates, crucially augmenting past research that has been more limited in global scope.

articles.title: Multilevel meta-analyses of emotional processing deficits associated with callous-unemotional (CU) traits: Do they differ by age and sex?
articles.authors: Emily C. Kemp; Paul Frick; Taylor Miller; Julianne Speck; David Gertz; Zeying Du
articles.abstract: Callous-unemotional (CU) traits, defined by deficient empathy and remorse, characterize a distinct subgroup of antisocial individuals with more severe behavioral problems and unique affective profiles. Two processes implicated in the development of CU traits are hyporeactivity to and inaccurate recognition of others’ emotions. Although many studies link CU traits to emotional processing deficits, findings have been inconsistent across age and sex. We conducted multilevel meta-analyses of emotional reactivity and recognition, accounting for age and sex as moderators, to clarify these discrepancies. A four-level meta-analysis indicated CU traits were negatively associated with emotional reactivity to both broad emotional stimuli (r = -.23, p < .0001; k = 106, n = 402) and distress-specific stimuli (r = -.22, p < .0001; k = 83, n = 234), with no moderation by age or sex. Similarly, a three-level meta-analysis showed CU traits were negatively associated with recognition accuracy for both broad facial emotions (r = -.09, p < .0001; k = 97, n = 437) and distress (e.g., fear, sadness; r = -.10, p < .0001; k = 60, n = 140). Sample age moderated broad (r = .003, p = .01) and distress (r = .004, p = .04) recognition deficits, such that effects diminished with sample age. These results have important implications for causal theories of CU traits and support emotional hyporreactivity as a core deficit that may cause delays in the development of emotion recognition abilities. Such developmental changes have implications for improving treatments for individuals with elevated CU traits.

articles_hidden.title: Investigating the association of linguistic distance with second and foreign language acquisition outcomes: A systematic review
articles_hidden.authors: Natalja Ulrich; Nils Jaekel
articles_hidden.abstract:
Ensuring equitable language learning support for everyone has become an urgent necessity, considering increasingly linguistically diverse classrooms. Understanding how linguistic backgrounds affect language learning outcomes is crucial, beyond the binary categories of non-native vs. native. Linguistic distance (LD) measures present more nuanced instruments to investigate the effect of the speaker's mother tongue. 
This systematic review examines research incorporating LD as a predictor of second or foreign language learning outcomes. Based on the search criteria, 35 articles were identified. The selected studies exhibit high variability in the tested languages, data samples, and methodological approaches. Among various LD measures, lexical distance and the index method were the most common approximations. 
Findings predominantly report a significant effect of LD on all language skills: speaking, writing, listening, and reading, regardless of tested language, age groups, data sample, and other nonlinguistic variables. Furthermore, the findings emphasize the importance of selecting LD measures following a skill-based approach.

articles_hidden.title: Social Context Moderates Mother-Infant Affective Synchrony in Everyday Life: An Ecological Momentary Assessment Study
articles_hidden.authors: Jennifer Ouyang; Sarvenaz Oloomi; Alexis Hernandez; Wenyi Xu; Alexa Monachino; Lauren C Shuffrey; Irene Tung; Santiago Morales
articles_hidden.abstract: Mother-infant affective synchrony, the moment-to-moment matching of mothers’ and infants’ emotions, is usually studied within the dyad when alone, yet everyday caregiving unfolds across varied social contexts. This study examined how momentary close company (partner, family member, or friend) relates to maternal affect and synchrony. Between September 2022 and September 2025, 253 mothers of infants aged 3–24 months (M = 9.4 months; 52.6% female; 56.7% Hispanic or Latinx) in Los Angeles, USA, rated their own and their infant’s affect up to six times daily for up to 14 days. Maternal and infant affect covaried at the same moment (negative β = 0.24; positive β = 0.28). Mothers reported higher positive and lower negative affect with a close companion or infant than alone or with distant company (acquaintances, coworkers, strangers). Negative synchrony was weaker with a close companion present (β = -0.05), although close company was unrelated to infant distress. Close company was also linked to higher infant happiness (β = 0.05) but not positive synchrony. Supplementary analyses found no lagged negative-affect effects and no partner-versus-family difference in the moderation. Maternal distress symptoms predicted higher chronic negative affect and stronger negative-affect inertia but not within-dyad dynamics. Early coregulation may extend beyond the dyad to the wider caregiving network.

articles_hidden.title: Predictor Selection for Doubly Robust Double/debiased Machine Learning Estimators for Causal Inference
articles_hidden.authors: Muwon Kwon; Peter M. Steiner
articles_hidden.abstract: Although machine learning (ML) facilitates causal effect estimation in high-dimensional settings, its naive application may introduce regularization and overfitting biases into effect estimates. Double/debiased ML (DML) mitigates these biases through Neyman orthogonality and sample splitting. While the local insensitivity of DML estimators to estimation errors in the propensity score (PS) and outcome models is well established, less attention has been given to improving the robustness of doubly robust DML estimators against model misspecification arising from ML-based predictor selection. To address this, we propose a union-based double post-Lasso estimator that re-estimates both the PS and outcome models using the union of their separately selected predictors. This approach eliminates differential predictor selection in the final models and reduces the risk of excluding important predictors from either model. Simulation results demonstrate that the proposed approach consistently reduces remaining confounding bias relative to approaches using separately selected predictor sets. The results also show that ML-based estimation does not uniformly outperform conventional doubly robust estimation and that post-Lasso reduces more confounding bias than Lasso. These findings highlight that reliable ML-based causal inference depends not only on the performance of the ML algorithm but also on how selected predictors are incorporated into causal effect estimation.

articles_hidden.title: The medial temporal lobe and the retention of scene memories across a one-week delay
articles_hidden.authors: Angelique I. Delarazan; Alexis N. Garcia; Ashley Huggins; Matthew D. Grilli
articles_hidden.abstract: Remembering everyday events involves retaining multiple components, including the scenes that provide the spatial and contextual setting in which events occur. The medial temporal lobe (MTL) supports scene construction and complex event memory. However, less is known about its contribution to retaining the details of an event’s scene over time, as scene information is typically embedded within narrative and event structures that are assessed for memory shortly after encoding. To examine scene memory retention, fifty-seven cognitively healthy older adults viewed 360-degree panoramic videos depicting real-world environments and freely recalled each scene shortly after viewing and again one week later. We tested whether individual differences in MTL volume were related to retention of scene memory and whether these relationships changed across the one-week delay. The proportion of episodic detail retrieved did not significantly change across the one-week delay, but the details recalled changed and became more participant specific, as measured by several measures of text-based similarity. Critically, relationships between MTL volume and scene memory also changed over time such that greater MTL volume was associated with being more consistent with what was originally recalled. Exploratory subregional analyses further showed that perirhinal cortex volume was robustly associated with the text-based similarity measures. These findings suggest that MTL is related to memory for the scene component of complex experience, particularly the ability to consistently recall the details of a scene over time.

articles_hidden.title: The time course of neural activity predictive of self-initiated movement
articles_hidden.authors: Lucas Jeay-Bizot; Mehmet Basbug; Uri Maoz; Robert Schapire; Aaron Schurger
articles_hidden.abstract: Decades of research have shown that early ramping activity is a very reliable antecedent of self-initiated movement. However, the dominant paradigm has been to only analyze data epochs culminating in movement, which discounts how often slow ramping might occur when no movement follows. To address this, we introduced a matched control condition that did not culminate in movement. We recorded electroencephalography data and compared these two conditions using a variety of powerful machine-learning classifiers. Although early ramping activity was present, it did not predict movement. Instead, classification accuracy rose abruptly about 100 ms before movement. By contrast, the traditional approach reproduced the spurious impression of early predictability. Our results resolve a long-standing controversy, showing that the neural commitment to act is a late-stage event consistent with the timing of conscious intention and the ability to inhibit movement. More broadly, our results show that a reliable antecedent is not necessarily a good predictor, underscoring the need for proper control conditions in time series analyses.

articles_hidden.title: Contexts, Risks, and Affordances among Autistic Adults Using Psychedelics for Therapeutic Purposes: A Naturalistic, Mixed-Methods Study
articles_hidden.authors: Alvita Sam; Alexander De Foe; Aspasia Stacey Rabba; Paul Liknaitzky; Kyle Greenway; Stephanie L. Lake; Philippe Lucas
articles_hidden.abstract:
Background: Autistic adults are under-investigated in psychedelic research, despite speculated elevated likelihood of substance use for therapeutic and recreational purposes.

Aims: This study explored contexts of naturalistic psychedelic use and wellbeing and mental health indicators in a group of Autistic adults using psychedelics for therapeutic purposes, and compared these with the broader population of naturalistic psychedelic users.

Methods: Secondary analysis of Global Psychedelic Survey 2023 data (N = 6,378) was undertaken with a sub-sample of naturalistic psychedelic users who self-indicated being Autistic adults who used psychedelics therapeutically. A convergent parallel mixed-methods study design investigated quantitative between-group differences in contexts of naturalistic psychedelic use and mental health indicators, and explored qualitative implications for wellbeing in the Autistic sub-sample.

Results: Compared with other psychedelic users (n = 6,166), the Autistic sub-sample (n = 212) reported higher rates of lifetime use of less common psychedelic substances and use in structured therapeutic settings, lower perceived psychedelic knowledge and experience, and greater prevalence of persisting hallucinations (65.09%) and clinically significant symptoms of anxiety (57.35%) and depression (60.66%) at the time of survey completion. Concurrently, three qualitative themes described largely beneficial, yet context-dependent implications for wellbeing within the Autistic sub-sample: Shifting Perspectives, Therapeutic Utility, and Conditional Affordances.

Conclusions: Integrated mixed-methods findings highlighted that wellbeing-related affordances of psychedelic use in the Autistic sub-sample were sometimes contingent on context and support, and adverse mental health indicators could co-exist with personal growth. Future research should further evaluate quality-of-life and adverse outcomes from psychedelic use in Autistic populations.

articles_hidden.title: How Are Daily Events Related to Subjective Well-Being? A Meta-Analytic Review of Intensive Longitudinal Studies
articles_hidden.authors: Lukas Schellenberg; Lina Hungerbuehler; Max Lustenberger; Wiebke Bleidorn; Peter Haehner
articles_hidden.abstract: Theory and research indicate that daily events—frequently occurring, time-discrete experiences that disrupt everyday life—are important predictors of momentary subjective well-being (SWB). However, findings about the associations between daily events and SWB vary substantially across studies, potentially reflecting differences in samples, event characteristics, or assessment methods. Moreover, it remains unclear whether these associations emerge at both the within- and between-person level and whether daily events prospectively predict SWB. To address these limitations, we conducted a preregistered systematic review and meta-analysis of within- and between-person associations between daily events and SWB across 217 intensive longitudinal studies (Ntotal = 48,311). Consistent with theoretical accounts, findings showed small-to-medium positive associations between daily uplifts and SWB, within (r = .16) and between persons (r = .21), and medium-to-large negative associations between daily hassles and SWB, within (r = −.18) and between persons (r = −.28). Moderator analyses further showed that these associations varied systematically depending on the type of daily event, its operationalization, and the examined SWB dimension. Furthermore, whereas daily events were associated with SWB when assessed concurrently, there was little evidence that these associations persisted into subsequent moments or days. Overall, the present meta-analytic review provides a comprehensive account of the associations between daily events and SWB. It indicates that daily uplifts and hassles are important correlates of SWB at both the within- and between-person level, but that their associations with SWB are relatively short-lived within individuals.

articles_hidden.title: Enhanced Sensitization Training in Aplysia Produces a Focused, Distinctive Set of Transcriptional Changes that Mostly Decays as Memory is Maintained
articles_hidden.authors: Irina Calin-Jageman; Jashui Zarate Torres; Theresa Wilsterman; Christian Gonzalez; Jaquelin Gutierrez; Carys McFaul; Nelly Musajeva; Zayra Juarez; Steven Proutsos; Octavian Calin-Jageman
articles_hidden.abstract: Forgetting remains a key puzzle in the neurobiology of memory.  One mysterious aspect of forgetting is its selectivity: most long-term memories are forgotten, becoming progressively less likely to be recalled, but extensive training can produce long-term memories that are readily expressed for a lifetime.  What are the molecular mechanisms through which training forestalls forgetting?  To explore this issue, we leveraged a well-documented training effect in long-term sensitization in Aplysia californica: a 1-day training protocol (standard) produces sensitization that is forgotten within 7 days, whereas 4-days of training (enhanced) produces sensitization that is durably expressed.  Here we confirm that enhanced sensitization training produces an enduring form of sensitization, with only subtle levels of forgetting for up to 11 days after training.  We then used microarray and qPCR to characterize the transcriptional changes occurring 1, 5, and 11 days after enhanced sensitization training.  We find that enhanced sensitization sustains only about 6% of the transcriptional changes induced by standard training, with many memory-linked transcripts showing no (ApCREB1) or significantly weaker (ApEgr) regulation with additional training.  Enhanced training also produces distinct activation of about 20 transcripts (relative to standard training), including up-regulation of putative homologs of genes related to synaptic plasticity (HINT1) and axon maintenance (zig-4).  Surprisingly, most of the transcriptional changes initially accompanying enhanced training fade rapidly, with the typical training effect at day 1 declining to 45% as strong by day 5 and then 28% as strong by day 11.  This decay is not complete, and we find sustained regulation of several transcripts, including some also persistently regulated by enhanced training (e.g. FMRFa and a putative GRIK1 homolog).  Overall, our results suggest that additional training produces a weaker but somewhat distinctive transcriptional response, most of which fades well before memory expression.

articles_hidden.title: From Access to Stabilisation: A Systems-Level Architecture of Cognitive Pathway Formation
articles_hidden.authors: Andrew Rockliffe
articles_hidden.abstract: Contemporary psychology provides well-developed accounts of framing, memory accessibility, salience, cognitive control, fixation, flexibility, and stabilisation. However, their functional integration during the formation and persistence of a cognitive pathway remains less clearly specified. This paper proposes a systems-level architecture in which cognition is understood as the currently active configuration of functional relationships within a highly interactive system. The current frame of mind represents this wider configuration, within which deployment profiles regulate the relative weighting and organisation of cognitive processes and capacities, memory access remains selective and state-dependent, and available information acquires differential functional prominence through salience. Candidate pathways are evaluated against current constraints and may become progressively stabilised, while feedback, changing conditions, closure modulation, and hysteretic dynamics can reinforce, modify, or reopen the developing state. The architecture distinguishes what is represented within the wider memory landscape from what becomes functionally accessible and subsequently salient, while treating stabilisation, closure, and reopening as dynamically related rather than as discrete terminal stages. Its contribution lies in specifying how interactions among these functions can generate qualitatively different outcomes, including efficient commitment, fixation, cognitive reorganisation, insight, persistence, and reopening. It therefore provides an analytical representation of a recursive, history-dependent system and generates testable questions concerning how cognitive pathways become accessible, influential, evaluated, sustained, revised, or reopened.

articles_hidden.title: The Effects of Cognitive Load on Intergroup Empathy Biases [Registered Report Stage 1, Version 2]
articles_hidden.authors: Jillian Elizabeth Franks; Jennifer Nadine Gutsell; Social Interaction and Motivation Lab
articles_hidden.abstract: Accurate and quick judgments of others’ mental and emotional states are crucial for social interaction. However, these judgments can be compromised by social biases, especially while cognitive demands are high and cognitive resources are low. Empathy is not always allocated to everyone equally, especially when the target is considered an outgroup member. One factor that may exacerbate such empathy biases is cognitive load, as cognitive load has been shown to increase ingroup biases and impair empathizing. This study investigates whether high cognitive load and racial outgroup membership interact, potentially worsening behavioral and self-reported indicators of empathy bias. To our knowledge, the present work is the first to directly manipulate cognitive load during intergroup empathizing, examining its effects on two distinct, yet interacting, routes of empathy—experience sharing and mentalizing. Mentalizing (cognitive empathy) and affective experience sharing (emotional empathy) activate different brain networks but interact during social situations, necessitating separate examination within the same paradigm. Using an empathy task designed to test racial empathy biases, we integrate behavioral and self-report measures to capture empathy dynamics in response to naturalistic stimuli. This approach allows us to test how group biases and cognitive load independently and jointly affect mentalizing and experience sharing.

articles_hidden.title: Youth First Supports Adolescent Wellbeing: A Longitudinal Cluster-Randomized Controlled Trial of a Teacher-Delivered School-Based Program in India
articles_hidden.authors: Peter L. Cooper; Katherine S. Leventhal; Gunjika Misra; Nandita Bhatla; Hari Shanker; Steve Leventhal
articles_hidden.abstract:
Adolescents face intersecting challenges that increase their risk of poor mental health, particularly in low- and middle-income countries, where 90% of adolescents live. School-based wellbeing programs offer a promising, cost-effective prevention strategy, but evidence from large-scale, government-delivered interventions with long-term follow-up is limited. We evaluated Youth First, an in-school wellbeing program delivered by teachers in rural government schools in two districts of Bihar, India.

We conducted a secondary analysis of a cluster-randomized controlled trial involving 70 schools. Sixty-nine schools provided baseline data from 5,445 Grade 7–8 students and were randomized to Youth First or standard education. Data were collected at baseline, 8 months, and 20 months. Primary outcomes were physical wellbeing, psychological wellbeing, and social and peer support; secondary outcomes included psychosocial and behavioral measures. Modified intention-to-treat analyses used mixed-effects difference-in-differences models with school and student random intercepts. Primary-outcome p-values were adjusted using the Benjamini-Hochberg procedure; secondary analyses were exploratory and unadjusted for multiplicity.

Youth First significantly improved social and peer support across multiple time points and cohorts after adjustment, with an additional effect on psychological wellbeing. Exploratory analyses found nominally significant effects on self-efficacy, empowerment, internalizing symptoms, and self-reported tobacco use, varying by grade and follow-up. Several effects persisted or emerged in the baseline Grade 8 cohort one year after program completion.

Youth First improved several adolescent outcomes during exposure and showed some sustained or delayed effects when delivered by government teachers through school systems in participating rural schools in Bihar.

articles_hidden.title: The effects of non-pharmacological school-based interventions on educational outcomes in children and young people with attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder: a meta-analysis
articles_hidden.authors: Dixiao Zhang; Dimitra Hartas; Olympia Palikara; Vasileios Sideropoulos
articles_hidden.abstract: Children and young people (CYP) with attention deficit hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) often face inequalities when accessing learning opportunities. The evidence base is mixed on the effectiveness of school-based interventions for CYP with ADHD on academic progress gains, improved attendance, and enhanced wellbeing. We conducted a meta-analysis to specify whether school-based interventions improve the educational outcomes of CYP with ADHD. Seven databases were searched until 2nd of October 2026. The review followed the PRISMA guidelines. Of the 2164 items identified, only 16 studies were included in our analysis as they met our inclusion criteria: a) CYP with ADHD aged 5-17 years old; b) school-based interventions; c) randomized controlled trials; and d) educational outcomes. Given the substantial heterogeneity across intervention types, the findings show an inconclusive pattern of what works and what doesn’t. Our main model demonstrated that overall school-based interventions showed a small effect on educational outcomes amongst CYP with ADHD. No significant moderators, such as intervention types and outcome domains, were detected. Future research should examine the broader contextual, educational, and environmental factors associated with better educational outcomes amongst CYP with ADHD, with the aim of developing more evidence-informed and targeted interventions.

articles_hidden.title: The Short General Attitudes Towards Artificial Intelligence Scale in Japan: Psychometric Validation and Exploratory Measurement Invariance with the Original UK Sample
articles_hidden.authors: Yu Kanno; Rina Kagawa
articles_hidden.abstract: As artificial intelligence (AI) becomes increasingly widespread, reliable measures of general attitudes toward AI are needed to understand public responses, and cross-national comparisons require evidence of measurement equivalence. This study addressed two objectives: validating the Short General Attitudes Towards Artificial Intelligence Scale (Short GAAIS-10; Schepman & Rodway, 2026) in Japan and exploring its comparability with the original UK sample. We translated the scale into Japanese (GAAIS-10-J) and examined its psychometric properties among 468 Japanese adults, including a one-month retest (N = 429). The original two-factor structure (Positive and Negative) received partial support, although some confirmatory factor analysis fit criteria were not met. Most items showed acceptable functioning, and both subscales demonstrated good internal consistency and adequate temporal stability. The two subscales captured related but distinguishable aspects of AI attitudes. Furthermore, the GAAIS-10-J explained additional variance in AI usage intention beyond perceived usefulness and ease of use. An exploratory comparison with the original UK sample (N = 500) approximately supported threshold and metric invariance but not full scalar invariance. Under a partial scalar invariance model, the Japanese sample had a higher latent Positive mean and a lower latent Negative mean than the UK sample, although these differences cannot be attributed directly to national or cultural factors. Overall, the GAAIS-10-J offers a brief measure of general AI attitudes in Japan, while the findings highlight the importance of accounting for measurement differences in cross-national comparisons.

articles_hidden.title: Gambling-related suicide and serious suicide attempts in the United Kingdom:  a psychological autopsy and qualitative investigation
articles_hidden.authors: Amanda Roberts; Jim Rogers; Richard J. E. James; Annie Ashton; Emily Beck; Pauline Turnbull; Gursharan Johal; Charles Ritchie; Tony Parente; Pauline Rivart
articles_hidden.abstract:
Background: Gambling-related harms are an important public health issue, with suicide representing one of their most serious potential consequences. However, although previous literature has identified elevated prevalence of suicidality among people who gamble, less is known about how gambling-related harms develop and subsequently relate to suicidal crisis.
Aims: To characterise the events and circumstances preceding gambling-related suicide and serious suicide attempts, and to examine the interacting socioecological, environmental and psychological processes through which gambling-related harms may have been linked to suicidal crisis.

Design: Exploratory multi-source psychological autopsy and qualitative inquiry, co-produced with people with lived experience. Narrative interviews were integrated, where available, with banking, gambling operator, health and coronial records. Interviews underwent iterative thematic analysis; records were analysed descriptively at case level using time series, case timelines and cross-case matrices.

Setting: United Kingdom. Study period: Jan 2023 to Dec 2025.

Participants/Cases: Twenty core cases were examined: 10 people who had died by gambling-related suicide, represented by close relatives or other affected people, and 10 people who had survived a serious suicide attempt associated with gambling-related harms. People who died were aged 19-46 years (9 male, 1 female); attempt survivors were aged 34-62 years (7 male, 3 female).
Measurements: Narrative interviews lasted approximately 3-4 hours and covered broad life history, key aspects of gambling history, industry interactions, suicidality, health, money, perceptions of gambling, and help-seeking and treatment. Record data were available for 14 of 20 cases. Sources included banking and operator activity, communications, health records and, in a small number, coronial or inquest material; coverage varied substantially between cases.

Results: Ten interconnected themes were identified: normalisation of gambling; the ‘responsible gambling’ narrative and individualisation of responsibility; industry practices and products; regulatory and policy weaknesses; lack of knowledge, information and understanding; shame, self-blame and stigma; money, debt and financial desperation; lack of recognition and ineffective treatment; lapse and recurrence; and entrapment and hitting the lowest point. Documentary records were consistent with interview findings, including intense or renewed gambling close to serious suicide attempts in several cases, substantial financial losses and borrowing, inducements and, in some cases, account restrictions followed by switching between operators.
Conclusions: In these cases, gambling-related suicidal crises involved interacting commercial, financial, psychological, relational and service-level processes. The findings identify potential opportunities for earlier recognition, stronger safeguards and sustained support.

articles_hidden.title: Feasibility and engagement of smartphone delivered yoga imagery with or without personalized avatars in residential substance use treatment: The AT-REACH nonrandomized pilot
articles_hidden.authors: Dennis McChargue; Byrav Ramamurthy; Wenyue Wang; Ashlin Ondrusek; Srikar Chanamolu; anna henson
articles_hidden.abstract: Background. Brief guided imagery may provide a practical way to rehearse a yoga experience between live sessions. We evaluated smartphone delivery and repeated use of yoga imagery and explored whether adding a personalized animated avatar was associated with different outcomes. Methods. This nonrandomized pilot enrolled 35 adults in four cohorts at residential substance use recovery facilities in Nebraska. Participants received an introductory yoga session and brief app delivered imagery practices, with three daily prompts. Thirteen participants received imagery with an animated avatar and 22 received imagery without the avatar. Allocation was by seat choice rather than a randomized sequence; the fourth cohort received the comparison condition only. We summarized app use over the first 28 days of logs, rated emotion changes around practice, and baseline to exit questionnaire outcomes. Results. All 35 initiated the app and 27 (77%) completed the exit assessment. Participants logged 2901 sessions, a median of 86 per person (interquartile range 62 to 104). At least three sessions were logged on 59% of days and at least one on 68%. The between group engagement effect was close to zero but imprecise (Hedges g = 0.03, 95% CI -0.66 to 0.71). Mean negative emotion intensity changed by -8.9 points on a 0 to 100 scale (95% CI -15.9 to -1.9). The baseline adjusted DERS total difference was 9.2 points (95% CI -6.7 to 25.2). The exploratory DERS Awareness change effect favored animated visual support (g = 0.89, 95% CI 0.06 to 1.73), but the cohort adjusted exit difference was smaller and imprecise (-1.30 points, 95% CI -5.05 to 2.46). Other questionnaire findings were mixed. Conclusions. The pilot documents repeated use of brief guided yoga imagery in residential recovery settings. It does not establish imagery efficacy, equivalence between formats, or an added benefit of animated visual support. Randomized evaluation with consistent assessment and complete delivery logs is warranted.

articles_hidden.title: Passive Smartphone-Based Digital Phenotyping for the Identification of PTSD Symptoms: Initial Validation of a Digital Behavioral Marker
articles_hidden.authors: Rony Kapel Lev-ari; Christian A. Webb; Doron Amsalem; Annika C. Sweetland; Yuval Neria; Milton Wainberg
articles_hidden.abstract:
Background: Passive smartphone-based digital phenotyping offers a scalable approach for continuous mental health assessment. Continuous passive monitoring may be particularly valuable for posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD), given fluctuating symptoms and the limitations of episodic clinical assessment. While previously validated for depression and anxiety, its application to PTSD remains limited. This study evaluated passive smartphone behavioral data for estimating PTSD symptom severity.
Methods: Adults (N = 176) completed the PTSD Checklist for DSM-5 (PCL-5) and passively contributed smartphone behavioral metadata via the Behavidence app. A Random Forest classifier using 44 behavioral features was developed to classify none (PCL-5 <31) versus severe (PCL-5 >61) PTSD symptom severity. The final model generated participant-level PTSD-related scores, which were evaluated across the full cohort. Feature importance was examined using Gini impurity and SHAP.
Results: In the holdout test set, the classifier achieved 80.3% accuracy, an AUC of 0.82, and 89.5% precision. When applied to the full cohort, participant-level MHSS values demonstrated a moderate positive correlation with continuous PCL-5 scores (r = 0.49, p < .001) and increased significantly across questionnaire-defined PTSD severity groups (F(3,172) = 24.06, p < .001, η² = 0.30). Feature importance analyses identified smartphone engagement, temporal usage patterns, and application-specific behaviors as the strongest contributors to model predictions.
Conclusions: Passive smartphone-based digital phenotyping demonstrated promising performance for identifying PTSD symptom severity. Participant-level MHSS values were associated with continuous and categorical measures of PTSD severity, supporting passive behavioral monitoring as a scalable complement to traditional PTSD assessment and longitudinal symptom monitoring.

articles_hidden.title: Do Students Experience Character Growth During Higher Education? Evidence From a Large, Multi-Institutional Study
articles_hidden.authors: Michael Prinzing; Juliette Lawson Ratchford
articles_hidden.abstract:
Decades of theoretical work in education research and developmental psychology suggest that students’ time in higher education is a critical period in their personal and moral development. Indeed, many institutions of higher education explicitly seek to promote students’ character growth. Yet empirical evidence regarding such growth during higher education remains limited. The present study (N = 473,627 undergraduates at 414 United States colleges and
universities) used mixed-effects models to examine students’ character growth across four years in higher education and to test whether such growth is moderated academic major, institutional characteristics, or students’ engagement in their campus communities. Results indicated that students do experience significant growth during their years in higher education. However, academic major and institutional type accounted for little variation. Instead, specific forms of community engagement, including participation in student organizations, mentorship and conversations about social and cultural issues, emerged as clear moderators. Alongside these theoretical implications, the findings have practical significance. The factors that appear to play the largest roles in shaping students’ growth are precisely those that staff, faculty, and administrators can influence, for example by prioritizing mentorship and promoting organizational involvement and dialogue across differences.

articles_hidden.title: Enhancing Clinical Psychological Science’s Role in Addressing Pressing Societal Issues: The Case Example of Firearm Violence Prevention
articles_hidden.authors: Edelyn Verona; Nicholas D. Thomson
articles_hidden.abstract: Clinical psychological science has contributed a range of methodological and treatment innovations that have improved human well-being. At the same time, our field can play a larger role in studying and addressing a range of societal problems and, crucially, in training future clinical scientists in this work. Applying the case example of firearm violence research, we describe ways to expand concentrations and training in “public” clinical psychological science to increase support for social problems research and its reach to impacted communities. We outline ways in which clinical science is well-positioned to advance such research and highlight potential reforms needed to create a sustainable pipeline of investigators interested in public health and clinical psychological science. The article presents an integrated agenda for building interdisciplinary collaborations, embedding cultural and policy competence into training, and ensuring sustained mentorship in the study and prevention of social problems, including firearm violence.

articles_hidden.title: Breaking the Cycle: Rewiring Negative Symptoms in Schizophrenia Through Physical Exercise
articles_hidden.authors: Bénédicte Thonon; Damien Brevers
articles_hidden.abstract: Individuals with schizophrenia commonly exhibit debilitating negative symptoms, including avolition and anhedonia, which represent a significant barrier to engagement in goal-directed behaviours, including physical exercise. They are less physically active than the general population, yet physical exercise is known to improve their symptoms. This narrative review investigates the bidirectional relationship between negative symptoms and physical activity. We propose that negative symptoms hinder engagement in physical activity by altering the cost-benefit analysis of exercise. This is exacerbated by deficits in anticipatory pleasure and reward learning, underpinned by dysfunctions within dopaminergic and glutamatergic circuitry which are critical for motivated behavior. We hypothesise that physical exercise can rewire these deficits through enhanced dopamine transmission, modulation of glutamatergic and GABAergic systems, and reduced inflammation. Furthermore, grounded in learning theories and adopting a cognitive-behavioural perspective, this review establishes a theoretical foundation for developing targeted interventions designed to enhance physical activity engagement in this population. We highlight that it is critical to ensure that physical activity is experienced as less effortful and more pleasurable than expected. By generating positive prediction errors (when the experience of exercise is less effortful or more pleasurable than anticipated) exercise helps individuals re-associate it with positive outcomes. Cognitive changes coupled with the biological effects of physical exercise on reward neural pathways are likely to have a synergistic effect, promoting a virtuous cycle of sustained engagement and symptom improvement.

articles_hidden.title: Hallucination-proneness is associated with more extreme social evaluations of external voices
articles_hidden.authors: Nadine Lavan; Georgina Needham-Bennett; Pedro Roberto Rojas Muñoz; Neve Elizabeth Greenfield
articles_hidden.abstract: Auditory verbal hallucinations are often experienced as the voices of entities who have a character and personality of their own. We asked whether hallucination-proneness in listeners affects how they evaluate the personality of external voices. 48 participants who self-reported a diagnosis of a psychotic disorder, and 50 participants without a similar diagnosis rated brief vowel recordings on attractiveness, competence, dominance, friendliness and trustworthiness. Hallucination-proneness was measured with the Cardiff Anomalous Perceptions Scale (CAPS) and the auditory hallucinations subscale of the Psychotic Symptom Rating Scales (PSYRATS-AH). Despite clearly higher symptom levels in listeners diagnosed with psychotic disorders, there was no group-level difference in average social trait evaluations, nor were average ratings associated with hallucination-proneness. There was, however, a numerical trend for listeners diagnosed with psychotic disorders to report more extreme social trait evaluations, where additionally, greater hallucination-proneness was also significantly associated with more extreme ratings across all social traits, on both measures. This association was, however, primarily present in controls but not in listeners diagnosed with psychotic disorders. Hallucination-proneness therefore appears to amplify, rather than directionally bias, social trait evaluations of voices. Our findings link proneness to experiencing internal voices, i.e. auditory verbal hallucinations, to how external voices are perceived. This finding is broadly consistent with previous work reporting that hallucination-prone individuals may be more likely to detect a signal (here: a salient social evaluation) in relatively ambiguous stimuli, speaking to mechanistic accounts that propose that stronger priors imbue stimuli with meaning.

articles_hidden.title: When Risk Factors Compete: A Machine Learning Approach to Identifying Antecedents of Adolescent Delinquency Across Domains, Development, and Gender
articles_hidden.authors: Matthew R. Cashman; Anna-Karin Andershed; Henrik Andershed; Frida Bood; Evelina Landstedt; Louise Frogner; Karin Hellfeldt
