articles_hidden.abstract: Risk factors for adolescent delinquency have been identified at multiple levels, from individual dispositions through family and school processes to ecological context, yet their relative importance remains unestablished. Which factors carry greatest weight, and when, has not been tested in simultaneous modelling. This study assessed 111 predictors spanning five domains across four developmental periods, predicting self-reported delinquency in mid-adolescence. Predictors were teacher- and parent-reported and the outcome adolescent self-reported. Participants were a Swedish population-based cohort followed from early childhood into adolescence (N = 2,121; 46.6% girls; mean age 3.86 years at baseline; 97.8% born in Sweden). Using machine learning techniques, random forests were estimated across the full span (AUC = .787, 95% CI [.747, .826]) and at each developmental period for boys and girls. Parent-rated conduct problems ranked among the leading predictors at every period, while caregiver emotional functioning carried greatest weight in early and late childhood before being displaced by dispositional and behavioral characteristics. Parent-rated social competence was the strongest protective factor. Associations were threshold-shaped, with the shift to elevated risk falling within the ordinary range of the measures. Gender differences in ranking were not supported by formal testing, which was low-powered.

articles_hidden.title: Using Language Models to Predict Values, Personality, Well-Being, and Meaning in Life From Ideal-Life Descriptions
articles_hidden.authors: Joffrey Fuhrer; Théo Desbordes
articles_hidden.abstract: Does the way we picture our ideal life reveal what we value, who we are, and how we thrive? In a preregistered study (N = 273), we tested whether free-form descriptions (median 109 words) and seven-keyword lists of one's ideal life predict a broad battery of psychological constructs: the Big Five, the ten Schwartz values, social dominance, political orientation, meaning in life, and subjective well-being. Using regularized linear probes on embeddings from transformer large language models (LLMs), inspired by model-interpretability research, we find that ideal-life narratives predict most constructs above chance in both conditions (mean r = 0.24 for free-form, mean r = 0.12 for keywords). This free-form advantage was concentrated on constructs people rarely name outright, such as achievement, benevolence, conformity, and emotional stability, implying that part of the signal lies in the manner of the telling rather than in the referents alone. Nineteen of the 24 constructs were recovered from roughly 120 words of text, a far broader battery than earlier language-based work, which has relied on much longer samples and focused on personality and well-being. Our approach offers an open, privacy-preserving alternative to zero-shot commercial LLMs, with comparable accuracy, no API cost, and freely released data and code.

articles_hidden.title: Social and psychological consequences of sustained civic engagement: Insights from the 2024/25 Student Blockades in Serbia
articles_hidden.authors: Ana Ivanov; Neda Janićijević; Milica Manojlović; Matija Gvozden; Vojin Simunović; Sanda Stanković
articles_hidden.abstract:
Objective: Student protest movements represent critical contexts for understanding how collective action shapes psychological development. This study examines the 2024/25 student blockades in Serbia, a unique, prolonged, nonpartisan, and leaderless mobilization unfolding across state universities under active government pressure and repression. Moving beyond purely political analyses, this research explores how participants made sense of their experiences, focusing on the intersections between collective engagement, identity transformation, social reconfiguration, and mental health.
Method: Adopting a qualitative framework grounded in phenomenological principles, data were gathered through semi-structured interviews (60–90 minutes) with a convenient snowball sample of 20 active undergraduate and graduate students (11 women, MAGE = 22.15, SDAGE = 1.69). Data were analyzed using reflexive thematic analysis, supported by MAXQDA 2022 software.
Results: The analysis identified three superordinate themes: (1) The Blockades as a Transformative Lived Space, reflecting changes in everyday routines and political subjectivity; (2) Reconfiguration of Social Relations through Collective Engagement, examining collective identity and moral commitment; and (3) Emotional Strain and Relational Buffering, reflecting experiences of anxiety, threat, and burnout, alongside resources that mitigated distress. 
Conclusion: The 2024/2025 Serbian student blockades constitute not only a political event but also an experience of sustained collective action that profoundly reshaped students' self-concept, social relations, and emotional functioning. Crucially, the interpersonal bonds that drive transformation also generate psychological strain, such as exhaustion and guilt. Acknowledging that the research team's shared socio-political positionality shaped these interpretations, the findings carry vital implications for universities, mental health practitioners, and civil society organizations.

articles_hidden.title: Classroom Group Meditation and Frontal EEG Power-Envelope Networks: A Twelve-Session Single-Channel Hyperscanning Study
articles_hidden.authors: GAO JUNLING; Yilin Zhang; Hank Leung; Kin Cheung Lee; Chun Chi Poon; Bonnie Wai Yan Wu; Hin Hung Sik
articles_hidden.abstract: Portable electroencephalography (EEG) allows neural activity to be recorded from whole classrooms, but correlated activity across students can arise from shared instructions, parallel changes in arousal or common artefact rather than interpersonal coupling, and dyads within one class are not independent observations. In this exploratory analysis, single-channel frontal EEG was recorded during eyes-closed rest and guided group meditation in twelve classroom sessions at four schools (194 students; 9–23 per session). For each session and band (alpha, theta, delta, beta), sparse partial-correlation networks among participants were estimated from 140 consecutive 2-s band-power values with the Graphical Lasso, using one condition-blind penalty for both conditions. The primary outcome, positive network strength, was compared between conditions with the session as the unit of inference, using exact sign-flip tests and false-discovery-rate control across bands. No band differed between meditation and rest (alpha: mean session difference = 0.00006, 95% CI [−0.00083, 0.00096], raw p = .887, q = .939). No band differed after calibration against circular-shift surrogates or when one penalty was applied to all sessions, and alpha stayed null when any one session was removed. Along the penalty path, 9 of the 12 sessions changed the sign of their own alpha difference. A tuning-free mean pairwise correlation, calibrated against circular-shift surrogates, also showed no condition difference in any band. These data do not show that brief group meditation changes interparticipant EEG organisation in classrooms, and they indicate that per-session penalised network summaries need penalty-path and tuning-free checks before they are interpreted.

articles_hidden.title: Registered Reports as the default pathway for confirmatory publication
articles_hidden.authors: Marta Topor; Joshua Silberstein Bamford; Marina Bazhydai; Zhang Chen; Hu Chuan-Peng; Clare Conry-Murray; Thiago Leiros Costa; Antica Culina; Mario Dalmaso; Zoltan Dienes
articles_hidden.abstract: By rewarding speed, volume, and coherent positive narratives, traditional publishing incentivizes questionable scientific practices and analytic flexibility. The latter especially contributes to blurring the distinction between exploration and confirmation, which inflates the apparent strength of confirmatory claims. This systemic issue has gone unchecked for decades, leaving the scientific community with a body of scholarly literature that is unreliable and lacking validity. Registered Reports (RRs) address problematic publishing practices by requiring a priori registration of confirmatory tests, which is peer-reviewed before the research begins (stage 1). The editorial acceptance of a stage 1 plan establishes a commitment to publication regardless of research outcomes. Publication remains, nonetheless, contingent on a second peer review and editorial scrutiny (stage 2) to verify that the approved plan was followed, all deviations were transparently disclosed and justified, confirmatory and exploratory claims are clearly delineated, and the integrity of the design was maintained. Meta-scientific comparisons indicate that RRs reduce outcome-based publication bias and improve methodological rigor without compromising perceived novelty. By making accepted RR protocols and their review history citable research outputs, RRs also strengthen recognition for peer-review work. In this perspective, we argue that RRs should become the primary mode of confirmatory publication moving forward.

articles_hidden.title: From Phonological Skills to Reading Fluency: The Mediating Role of Reading Prosody
articles_hidden.authors: Petra Kóródi; Ferenc Honbolygó
articles_hidden.abstract:
Purpose: The development of reading fluency relies on phonological skills and prosodic competence, but evidence about the developmental mechanisms underlying this relationship remain scarce. Previous research has relied on subjective rating scales or adult-based acoustic comparisons, mostly in stress-timed languages. This study investigated whether objective acoustic markers of oral reading prosody mediate the relationship between cognitive skills (phonological awareness [PA] and rapid automatized naming [RAN]) and reading fluency in a syllable-timed language.
Method: The sample consisted of 56 typically developing, Hungarian-speaking primary school children (Mage = 8.96 years, 55,36% boys) who completed standardized cognitive assessments. Prosodic competence was measured by comparing acoustic features from an oral reading task against each child's own prosodic imitation baseline, using dynamic time warping to align melodic and rhythmic contours. Data were analyzed using path analysis.
Results: Temporal features, especially tempo stability, emerged as the strongest predictor of reading fluency, whereas melodic and rhythmic markers added no unique variance. Path analysis revealed that RAN predicted reading fluency directly, while PA's contribution was entirely indirect: stronger PA reduced pausal intrusions, which maintained temporal stability and, through it, reading fluency.
Conclusion: PA appears to influence reading fluency indirectly through sequential, temporal prosodic execution. In syllable-timed languages like Hungarian, sentence-level temporal mechanisms may carry the primary explanatory weight, highlighting that reading development models should account for the specific rhythmic properties of the reader's native language.

articles_hidden.title: A Computational Swinging Lexical Network: Cohort Concentration Predicts Semantic Interference in a Large-Scale Picture–Word Interference Dataset
articles_hidden.authors: Louis Schiekiera; Rasha Abdel Rahman; Alissa Melinger; Vincent Gruber; Fritz Guenther
articles_hidden.abstract: The Swinging Lexical Network (SLN) model explains semantic context effects in word production through the lexical cohort that a target and distractor co-activate: whether naming is facilitated or slowed depends on the balance between semantic priming and lexical competition within this cohort. As a verbal theory the SLN leaves open what counts as a competitor: any co-activated word, or only words whose activation stands out. We implemented the SLN computationally, letting activation spread through a 30,000-word distributional semantic network. From this process we derived two measures. Cohort concentration is the degree to which co-activation falls on a few words instead of being spread thinly across many. The swing is how much the activation pattern still changes over later spreading steps. In a harmonized picture--word interference dataset of 392,156 trials from 86 English and German experiments, cohort concentration was the only semantic predictor with a reliable effect in both languages: naming was slower when a few words stood out as strongly activated competitors and faster when activation was diffuse. Competitors are thus the words whose activation stands out from the background, not every word that receives some activation. Adding the swing improved fit, but its effect could not be separated from cohort concentration, with which it was strongly correlated. Because spreading converges on the same network-wide state for every word pair, later steps largely re-express the initial cohort. In line with the SLN, our computational implementation shows that semantic interference depends on how co-activation is distributed across the cohort.

articles_hidden.title: Self-Identity and Trauma- and Stressor-related Psychopathology: A Systematic Review
articles_hidden.authors: Kari Ellen James; Blake M McKimmie; Fiona Maccallum
articles_hidden.abstract: Across the past two decades, there has been increasing interest in the role self-identity may play in the development and maintenance of trauma- and stressor-related psychopathology. Shaped by foundational theoretical models, this interest has led to an expanding yet heterogeneous body of literature dominated by a focus on event centrality and characterized by overlapping concepts and conceptual ambiguity. This systematic review aims to synthesize this literature to enhance conceptual clarity and guide the field’s development. 36 studies (77.8% traumatic stress, 22.2% prolonged grief) representing 7,488 individual participants met inclusion criteria. Three overarching self-identity constructs were identified through a synthesis of the literature: self-consistency, self-complexity, and self-identity processing. Greater self-consistency and self-complexity were generally associated with less severe traumatic stress and prolonged grief symptoms. There were too few studies to draw meaningful conclusions about self-identity processing. Notably, almost all studies employed cross-sectional correlational designs, limiting any conclusions about causal relationships. Further, most studies relied on self-report and so are vulnerable to motivational reporting biases. And while many constructs reflected proposed theoretical mechanisms, integration with broader models and literature was limited, constraining cumulative theoretical development. Culturally relevant self-construal emerged as a potentially important moderating factor, underscoring a need for more cross-cultural research. Limitations of the current review notwithstanding, we hope that providing greater conceptual clarity regarding theoretically important but less-studied aspects of the self will provide a useful framework for guiding future research and theory development, and, ultimately, improve outcomes for those living with these conditions.

articles_hidden.title: Trauma, Cannabis Use and Attenuated Psychotic Symptoms: A Mediation Model in the Uruguayan General Population
articles_hidden.authors: Richard Rodriguez; Celia Ceballos-Munuera; Paul Ruiz; Juan F. Rodriguez-Testal; Álvaro Cabana
articles_hidden.abstract:
Abstract
Background: At-risk mental states (ARMS), involving subclinical attenuated psychotic experiences, occur in the general population with persistence rates above 30%, and may substantially affect quality of life, well-being and global functioning. Cannabis use has been linked to the onset, persistence and intensity of attenuated psychotic symptoms, whereas other evidence identifies trauma as a mediating factor. This study examined the potential effect and degree of interaction of cannabis use patterns in a general population sample with a history of traumatic experiences during childhood and adolescence. Methods: A selective ex post facto cross-sectional survey design was used. Adults residing in Uruguay with no prior psychopathological diagnosis (n = 652, 66.3% women, M = 31.9 years, SD = 8.5) completed a controlled online survey assessing traumatic experiences, negative symptoms, aberrant salience, ideas of reference and cannabis use patterns. Results: Statistically significant correlations confirmed a dual interaction of traumatic experiences, and of the frequency and grams of cannabis used, on attenuated psychotic symptoms. Traumatic experiences explained R2 = .202 of the variance in attenuated psychotic symptomatology, more than the dose (R2 = .14) and frequency (R2 = .048) of cannabis use. Combining the trauma effect with both use-pattern effects yielded a model with better fit and greater explained variance (R2 = .252). Conclusions: Traumatic experiences during childhood and adolescence are positively associated with cannabis use and, to a greater extent, with attenuated psychotic symptoms (ARMS) such as ideas of reference, aberrant salience and negative symptoms, showing greater explanatory power than cannabis use.

articles_hidden.title: Beyond validity: Empirical investigations of the statistical power of da in Recognition Memory
articles_hidden.authors: Adva Levi; Caren M. Rotello; Yonatan Goshen-Gottstein
articles_hidden.abstract: Recognition memory relies on sensitivity measures to identify memory effects (i.e., differences in sensitivity). Alas, all commonly used sensitivity measures (d′, A′, Percent correct, and Pr) have been shown to be confounded with response bias, raising serious validity concerns for the literature. da, a signal-detection measure grounded in the Unequal-Variance Signal-Detection model, has been proposed as a bias-independent alternative. Yet, establishing da as the gold standard for measuring memory effects requires demonstrating not only that it produces low rates of false discoveries, but also that it has sufficient statistical power to detect genuine differences in sensitivity. The low false discovery rate has been established with both simulated and large-scale experiments (Levi, Danino, et al., 2026; Levi, Rotello & Goshen-Gottstein, 2026).  Here, we examined the estimated power of da using empirical data from 960 online participants who completed a recognition task under two sensitivity conditions (repetition manipulation). We used resampling techniques to test power levels for multiple sample sizes and found that da achieved significance rates comparable to those of the commonly-used measures, regardless of the statistical test or effect size. The typical 80% power threshold was achieved with approximately 48 participants. Together with our previous findings, these results establish da as a valid and statistically powerful measure, thus confirming the recommendation to adopt da as the measure of choice in recognition memory research.

articles_hidden.title: Perceptual similarity landscape differs between young and clinically unimpaired older  adults and contributes to long-term memory precision
articles_hidden.authors: Haopei Yang; Mingjian He; Angela Han; Dulce Karina Pimentel-Hurlburt; Julia Glueck; Zoe Katherine Jung; Ryan J. Southward; Gayle K. Deutsch; Niyatee Samudra; Patrick L. Purdon
articles_hidden.abstract:
The precision of memory for event features is lower in older relative to young adults. Recent 
studies that examined continuous reproduction data with a mixture model –– which estimates 
two parameters putatively reflecting reduced fidelity/precision and outright forgetting –– suggest 
age-related memory decline is associated with a selective or larger reduction in mnemonic 
precision vs. forgetting. However, emerging evidence indicates that performance on continuous 
reproduction paradigms depends not just on memory, but also on the psychophysical similarity 
function (PSF) of the perceptual feature space, which may also change with age. Using a recently 
developed one-parameter statistical model of continuous reproduction memory data that 
mechanistically accounts for the empirically measured PSF, we examined whether age-related 
differences in continuous reproduction data are at least partially explained by age-related 
differences in perception. Young adults (age 18-25 yrs, N = 55) and clinically unimpaired older 
adults (age 68-86 yrs, N = 54) with normal color vision performed (a) a continuous reproduction 
task probing long-term memory for object color, (b) a Likert color similarity judgement task, and 
(c) a color matching task. We first replicated previous findings of age-related differences in 
memory precision for the colors of previously encountered objects and identified age-related 
changes in color perception on the similarity and matching tasks. We then characterized the age-
group specific perceptual landscape by constructing the PSF using the similarity task data. 
Subsequent model comparison revealed that for both age groups, the more parsimonious one-
parameter model, which accounts for the age-group specific PSF, explained continuous 
reproduction data better than the mixture model. Notably, the PSFs differed between age groups, 
and the difference was not explained by individual differences in response bias or trial-history 
effects. When we replaced the PSF estimated from older adults’ perceptual data with that 
estimated from the younger adults in the one-parameter model, it produced a worse fit to older 
adults’ continuous reproduction data compared to the model with the age-group appropriate PSF, 
further supporting a link between age-related changes in perception and the precision of episodic 
memory.

articles_hidden.title: AI-Powered Prevention and Early Intervention for Stress, Depression, and Anxiety: A Randomized Clinical Trial
articles_hidden.authors: Julie Youko Anne Cachia; Xuan Zhao; Wenxi Pu; Chi Liao; merel Keijsers; Julian De Freitas; Rebecca Fortgang
articles_hidden.abstract: Randomized evidence for purpose-built generative AI mental health support remains limited. In this preregistered trial, 1,137 unscreened university students were assigned to 6 weeks of Flourish or care as usual. All three primary endpoints were met, with more favorable trajectories for perceived stress (β = -0.03, p = 0.010), depressive symptoms (β = -0.03, p = 0.006), and anxiety symptoms (β = -0.04, p = 0.001). Benefits were observed across baseline severity, with less deterioration at low severity and greater improvement at elevated severity. Among participants with elevated symptoms, improvements were larger with Flourish for depression (d = 1.03 vs 0.56) and anxiety (d = 0.91 vs 0.60), with meaningful improvements of 52.3% vs 31.7% and 50.6% vs 38.1%, respectively. Reductions in perceived stress emerged as one potential pathway to broader improvements in depressive and anxiety symptoms. These findings support scalable first-line AI support spanning prevention and early intervention.

articles_hidden.title: Clustering of differential conditioned response trajectories using skin conductance: Are fear conditioning studies affected by pre-existing characteristics?
articles_hidden.authors: Luke John Ney; Matthew Greaves; Matthew Paul O'Donohue; Trevor Steward; Yi Wang; Madeline Jarvis; Rachel Patterson; Camilla Luck; Ottmar Lipp
articles_hidden.abstract: Recent research suggests that responses during experimental fear conditioning follow distinct latent trajectory classes. Computational reinforcement learning models can be used to infer latent learning processes during the task (e.g., learning rates and prediction-error sensitivity) that may help explain these classes. The present study re-analysed previously published and unpublished datasets to examine patterns of fear learning using skin conductance responses (SCRs) in a large sample of healthy participants. Data were aggregated from 12 fear conditioning experiments (N = 1,083; Mage = 20.72 years), encompassing acquisition, extinction, and return-of-fear phases. Using k-means clustering, we identified solutions comprising either two or three distinct response profiles. Across clusters, approximately half of participants showed minimal differential SCRs, while the remaining participants exhibited higher conditioned responding during acquisition, with subsets differing in whether fear returned following extinction. Cluster membership was significantly predicted by gender, current anxiety levels, post-acquisition conditioned stimulus pleasantness ratings, and Bayes factors quantifying evidence for model-based learning. Comparison of reinforcement learning models indicated that a latent cause model provided a superior account of SCR data relative to Rescorla–Wagner, Pearce–Hall, and hybrid models, with latent cause parameters differing by cluster and gender. The clustering data provide preliminary evidence that SCR outcomes in fear conditioning studies may be disproportionately influenced by a minority of participants with specific pre-existing characteristics, rather than reflecting uniform learning processes. Moreover, the results provide support for latent cause theories of fear learning and highlight the value of combining clustering and computational approaches to better understand individual differences in fear acquisition, extinction, and relapse.

articles_hidden.title: Associations Between Motives and Emotion Regulation Strategy Use in Everyday Life
articles_hidden.authors: Valentina Bianchi; Tyler Thorne; Elise Katherine Kalokerinos; Felicity Angelopoulos; Marina Milyavskaya
articles_hidden.abstract: Theories suggest that capturing people’s motives (the ‘why’) for regulating allows for a better understanding of how people choose to regulate their emotions. Yet, little empirical research systematically examines the link between motives and regulation strategies. Addressing this gap, we conducted an experience-sampling study to: 1) capture the prevalence of a wide range of regulatory motives (hedonic, instrumental) in everyday life and (2) test whether motives were associated with the selection of six regulation strategies, controlling for affect intensity. Data were collected in Australia in 2024, from an adult community sample (NID=303;  Nobs=3496; Mage = 26.11; 80% women, mostly identifying as East Asian and South-East Asian). Hedonic motives were most frequent, but instrumental motives were also common. Regulatory motives showed distinct strategy selection profiles: prohedonic motives were linked with greater distraction and cognitive reappraisal, whereas contrahedonic motives were rare, and only predicted greater rumination. Different instrumental motives were differentially associated with the use of specific strategies. Only cognitive strategies (reappraisal and rumination) were linked to multiple motives, being significantly associated with prohedonic, contrahedonic (rumination), personal performance, social, epistemic, and eudaimonic motives. By investigating the momentary association between a broad range of motives and regulation strategies, this work suggests that emotion regulation strategies are associated not only with what people feel, but also with why they regulate. Future empirical work should explicitly consider individuals’ regulatory motives, rather than assuming regulatory effectiveness based on hedonic motives.

articles_hidden.title: A Benchmark for Gaze-Based Target Detection in Immersive Virtual Reality: Effects of Eccentricity, Size, and Speed on Observation and Detection Dynamics
articles_hidden.authors: Arwa Leilah Adib; Margaret E. Sereno; David Schwarz
articles_hidden.abstract: Virtual reality enables studying active visual search and gaze behavior under naturalistic, free-viewing conditions while preserving experimental control. However, free head-eye coordination, extended 3D space, dynamic target trajectories, and headset-specific field of view and eye-tracking constraints mean that findings from traditional 2D paradigms cannot be assumed to generalize to immersive environments. Interpreting gaze-based outcomes in VR requires bench-marks that establish how basic target properties influence detection. We used target eccentricity, size, and speed as benchmark predictors of visual detection in an immersive VR coin-foraging task. Using in-headset eye-tracking, participants guided a gaze-controlled avatar to collect coins that varied in gaze-relative eccentricity, size, and speed. We modeled gaze-based observation probability, observation latency, dwell time, gaze-coin angular distance, and saccade dynamics. Observation probability was analyzed using mixed-effects logistic regression, whereas latency was analyzed with a censoring-aware Cox framework that retained never-detected coins. Eccen-tricity and size showed the clearest benchmark effects. Peripheral and small coins were less like-ly to be detected. Speed’s role was more nuanced. Although slow coins were detected more of-ten in a binary model, this advantage did not persist in a censoring-aware survival analysis, suggesting that speed influenced the opportunity for observation more than momentary salience. Consistent with this interpretation, slow coins produced longer dwell times, and gaze-coin an-gular distance and saccade measures indicated that target properties shaped both the geometry and effort for acquisition. These findings establish a feature-based benchmark for gaze-based de-tection in immersive visual search and demonstrate the importance of modeling missed targets as censored detection opportunities.

articles_hidden.title: Navigating Autistic College Students’ Career Development: A Capability-Oriented Perspective on Agency and Advocacy
articles_hidden.authors: Yilun Jiang; Karly Ball Isaacson; Bradley E. Cox; Brett Ranon Nachman
articles_hidden.abstract: Autistic college students navigate career development through their interests and strengths, while encountering deficit-oriented assumptions about autism. Research on autistic students’ career development usually focuses on career support and skill development, while limited studies have examined how they pursue career pathways from a strengths-based perspective. Drawing on a secondary analysis of semi-structured interviews from a national mixed-methods study (n = 36), we examined how autistic college students in four-year U.S. colleges navigate career development. Applied thematic analysis identified three themes: participants developed purpose-driven career goals through long-standing interests, lived experiences, and community exposure; navigated judgments about capability and professional fit across academic and career contexts; and assembled career support across career centers, faculty, and autism support groups. Our findings highlight autistic participants’ capability to explore career pathways that reflect their interests and goals and suggest an agency-beyond-advocacy interpretation, in which agency refers to broader forms of action through which students shape their career development and advocacy represents one important form of agency. Finally, we offer suggestions for universities and employers to develop resources more tailored to autistic students’ career goals and needs.

articles_hidden.title: Predicting and explaining public support for environmental policies: A comparative analysis of two theories
articles_hidden.authors: Violetta Vysevkova; Claire Farrow; Jason Thomas; James Reynolds
articles_hidden.abstract: Environmental policies are crucial for mitigating climate change and protecting people’s health. Public opposition, however, often undermines their adoption and success. Theories that seek to explain and predict policy support and opposition are insufficiently tested or have not received empirical support. This study tested how well one influential theory, and one new theory explain and predict support for environmental taxes on frequent flying, fast fashion, and red meat. These two theories are the Value-Belief-Norm (VBN) theory and the Integrative Public-Policy-Acceptance (IPAC) framework. A cross-sectional online survey was conducted with a nationally representative sample of adults in the United Kingdom (N = 1,270). Data were analysed using partial least squares structural equation modelling. The IPAC model explained a substantially greater proportion of variance in support for all three policies (R2 = .81–.85) than the VBN model (R2 = .20–.26). The IPAC model also produced practically meaningful predictions of policy support (RMSE/MAE = 0.63–0.91), whereas the VBN model did not (RMSE/MAE = 1.40–1.78). The direct comparison confirmed the IPAC is the superior model of policy support (BICIPAC < BICVBN). Several propositions of the IPAC framework were not supported, highlighting the need for further tests and perhaps refinements to its structure. To enhance the precision of explanations and predictions, we recommend that theories of policy attitude include policy-specific beliefs, such as perceived policy fairness and effectiveness—the strongest determinants of policy support. Other relevant factors can be considered in assumptions that supplement theories for application in specific contexts.

articles_hidden.title: A Person-Centered Analysis of Change in Supports for Child Welfare-Involved Families and Caregiver and Child Outcomes
articles_hidden.authors: Qiong Wu; Lenore M McWey; Melissa Radey; Ming Cui
articles_hidden.abstract: Families involved with the U.S. child welfare system are overwhelmingly lower-resourced and often experience multiple hardships, which can adversely affect mental health. Research indicates that public, private, and child welfare system supports may individually shape caregiver and child well-being. Conversely, loss or insufficiency of support is linked to more family hardship and worse parent and child mental health. With data from the National Survey of Child and Adolescent Well-being II, we used a person-centered approach to examine longitudinal configurations of public, private, and child welfare system supports over three years and caregiver and child outcomes. Results revealed distinct patterns of family supports over time, and that public and private supports tended to be stable, but child welfare system supports were likely to change over time. Mean difference comparisons across classes generally revealed that parents with strong private safety nets reported better mental health outcomes for themselves and lower behavioral problems for their children compared to those with high public and low private supports. Findings from this study have practical implications for supporting families involved with the child welfare system.

articles_hidden.title: The Structure and Content of Meaning in Speech Reflects Mental Health
articles_hidden.authors: Luke Leckie; Alicia Meuret; Thomas Ritz; Olivia Losiewicz; Michelle G. Craske; Jacob G. Foster
articles_hidden.abstract: Mental health shapes the progression and content of thought. Studies have linked depression, anxiety, and stress with repetitive negative thoughts, but it remains unclear whether these disturbances are reflected in the structure of an individual's speech. We introduce an approach to quantify the structure of thought as expressed in language, applying it to memory recountings from 82 individuals across six psychotherapy sessions. We model each recounting’s semantic progression with contextual embeddings, and use persistent homology to identify loops of meaning, as recountings circle back upon themselves. More loops are associated with depression, anxiety, stress, and negative affect, and with negative self-referential language, implicating them as geometric markers of negative fixation and rumination. Semantic content also relates to mental health. However, neither semantic structure nor content mediate therapeutic improvement. These findings reveal that the semantic structure of speech offers a quantitative window into thought disturbances in depressive and anxiety disorders.

articles_hidden.title: Attentional network processing in children and adults shows comparable behavioural effects but distinct ERP and time–frequency activity
articles_hidden.authors: Praghajieeth Raajhen Santhana Gopalan; Otto Loberg; Jarmo Hamalainen; Paavo H. T. Leppänen
articles_hidden.abstract: Visual attention comprises alerting, orienting, and executive-control networks. Although these networks are behaviourally evident in childhood, age differences in the neural processes supporting them remain unclear. Typically developing 12–13-year-old children (n = 77) and 19–33-year-old adults (n = 21) performed the Attention Network Test while electroencephalography (EEG) was recorded. Behavioural performance was assessed using reaction time and accuracy. Neural processing was examined using event-related potentials (N1 and P3 amplitudes and latencies) and induced time–frequency analyses of theta (4–7 Hz), alpha (8–12 Hz), and beta (13–25 Hz) band activity. Significant alerting, orienting, and executive-control effects were observed in reaction time, with children responding more slowly overall than adults. Children showed longer N1 latencies than adults during the orienting comparison, indicating slower early target-related processing. Alerting cues increased target-related N1 amplitudes similarly in both groups. Adults, but not children, showed smaller P3 amplitudes for incongruent than congruent trials, whereas children showed larger P3 amplitudes overall, suggesting age-related differences in conflict-related processing. Time–frequency analyses showed that alerting modulated theta-, alpha-, and beta-band activity similarly in both groups. Orienting-related theta activity differed between age groups, with children showing higher theta power for spatial- than centre-cue trials. Alpha-band activity also differed between orienting conditions similarly in both groups. These findings indicate that children and adults can show comparable behavioural attentional network effects despite differences in neural processing. The results further suggest that electrophysiological measures of attentional processing show age-related differences beyond late childhood.

articles_hidden.title: Neuroscience-Informed Psychoeducation for Epilepsy: A Shared Language for Integrated Care
articles_hidden.authors: Islam Elbanna; Yamane A. Makke
articles_hidden.abstract:
Epilepsy is among the most burdensome neurological disorders worldwide, with an impact that extends far beyond seizure frequency alone. Depression, anxiety, cognitive impairment, and internalized stigma affect a substantial proportion of individuals with epilepsy, yet these comorbidities remain systematically undertreated in routine neurological care. Conventional psychoeducation, largely centered on passive information delivery, has shown limited effectiveness in addressing the psychological and social complexities of living with epilepsy. Neuroscience-Informed Psychoeducation for Epilepsy (NIPE) offers a fundamentally different approach: one that translates the neuroscience of seizure generation, network dysfunction, and neuroplasticity into accessible frameworks, shifting patients from passive recipients of information to active, metacognitively engaged participants in their own care.
This chapter presents NIPE as both a clinical framework and an integrative layer across the continuum of epilepsy management. Beginning with the neurobiological mechanisms underlying seizures and epileptogenesis, it highlights how the same neural networks implicated in ictal activity also contribute to the psychiatric and cognitive comorbidities that shape patients’ daily experiences. It further examines how NIPE interfaces with evidence-based psychological interventions, pharmacologic education, neuromodulation, epilepsy surgery, and the management of refractory epilepsy, as well as the unique needs of women and other populations with distinct clinical considerations.
In addition, the chapter explores the digital expansion of NIPE, including adaptive telehealth platforms, wearable biosensors, digital phenotyping, and the emerging role of artificial intelligence in tailoring psychoeducational delivery. Importantly, it addresses current limitations and ethical considerations with transparency, including the absence of standardized NIPE protocols and the relative scarcity of randomized controlled trials specifically within epilepsy populations.
The chapter concludes with a forward-looking perspective on the infrastructure, research agenda, and cross-disciplinary collaboration required to embed NIPE into routine epileptology practice. NIPE is positioned not as an adjunct to epilepsy care, but as a unifying framework, a shared language that enables truly integrated, patient-centered care.

articles_hidden.title: Who cares about human rights and the environment? Replicating and extending McFarland’s structural model
articles_hidden.authors: Taciano L Milfont; Felipe Vilanova
articles_hidden.abstract: Why are some people more committed than others to protecting human rights worldwide? McFarland (2010) proposed that people high in Right-Wing Authoritarianism (RWA) and Social Dominance Orientation (SDO) are less committed to universal human rights partly because they are more ethnocentric and identify less with humanity as a whole. We tested this model in a larger sample of US adults (N = 512). The core model was supported: RWA and SDO were linked to greater ethnocentrism, which was associated with weaker identification with all humanity (IWAH) and human-rights commitment, whereas IWAH was associated with stronger commitment. As McFarland found, SDO also had a direct negative association with commitment that empathy did not explain. However, McFarland’s original hypothesized model fit significantly better than his final trimmed model. Two previously excluded paths emerged in our larger sample, linking SDO with lower IWAH and RWA with weaker human-rights commitment. Extending the model to environmentalism revealed several similar associations, but poor overall model fit. Our findings support McFarland’s framework while refining its specification and suggesting limits to its generalizability across domains and national contexts.

articles_hidden.title: The longform recordings era: The importance of scientific communities in advancing language development research
articles_hidden.authors: Federica Bulgarelli; Monica E Ellwood-Lowe; Naja Ferjan Ramirez; Hillary Ganek; Jessica Elizabeth Kosie; Alfa Montiel; Ashlie H Pankonin; Ritwika VPS; Eva Ståhlberg-Forsén; Sarah Surrain
articles_hidden.abstract: Longform recordings — passive audio recordings that capture the audio environment around a child, often for a full day — contribute to our understanding of language acquisition. This manuscript focuses on the practice of investigating children’s natural language experiences using longform recordings and the contributions of international scientific consortia to advancing this methodology. Drawing on a sys-tematic literature search identifying 378 studies, we describe the history of longform recordings, syn-thesize key research findings, and identify opportunities for growth. Further, we describe the impact of international collaborative communities on this work. In particular, we highlight the role of DARCLE (Daylong Recordings of Children’s Linguistic Environments), an international consortium of researchers that, starting in 2014, has spurred major advances in the field, including data sharing platforms and annotation norms, open-source technology for quantifying children’s language environments, and a set of best practices for conducting this research in diverse environments. This community of open discus-sion and data sharing serves as a model for advancing rigor, accessibility, and scale. We conclude with recommendations both to further strengthen research with longform recordings and for international research communities across disciplines.

articles_hidden.title: Judging orientation does not elicit the Spatial-Numerical Association of Response Codes: Testing the Neural Overlap Hypothesis
articles_hidden.authors: Valter Prpic; Stefano Pileggi; Alberto Mariconda; Serena Mingolo; MAURO MURGIA
articles_hidden.abstract: According to the neural overlap hypothesis (Fias et al., 2001), numerical magnitude may influence performance in a non-semantic task when the processing of task-relevant and task-irrelevant information recruits overlapping neural structures. Specifically, because number and orientation processing both engage parietal regions, the account predicts a SNARC effect during orientation judgments, whereas effects should be weaker in tasks with less parietal involvement, such as colour judgments. However, only a few studies have attempted to replicate the original findings. Here, we conducted a large-sample replication of the line orientation task introduced by Fias et al. (2001, Experiment 4) and included letters as a complementary condition. Across two experiments, conducted online and in the laboratory, we consistently failed to detect a SNARC effect for numbers or a SNARC-like effect for letters. A cumulative analysis likewise provided no evidence for either association. These findings fail to replicate a key result supporting the neural overlap hypothesis and suggest that shared parietal processing may not give rise to spatial-numerical associations as robustly as previously assumed.

articles_hidden.title: EEG in Parkinson’s Disease: Mechanisms, Biomarkers and Translational Opportunities
articles_hidden.authors: Sümeyye Özdemir; Sahar Allouch; Manon Auffret; Mahmoud Hassan; Marc Vérin
articles_hidden.abstract: Parkinson’s disease (PD) is characterized by nigrostriatal dopaminergic degeneration and basal ganglia dysfunction, yet these pathophysiological abnormalities alone do not fully explain its heterogeneous motor and non-motor manifestations. Over recent decades, electroencephalography (EEG) has evolved from a primarily descriptive technique into a quantitative approach for investigating cortical electrophysiological dynamics associated with PD. Accumulating electrophysiological evidence implicates altered oscillatory synchronization and interactions across cortical and subcortical circuits in PD-related dysfunction, suggesting disturbances in the temporal coordination of neural activity. Emerging approaches, including large-scale datasets, multimodal integration, individualized modeling and wearable EEG technologies, offer opportunities for physiological phenotyping and real-world monitoring. However, methodological heterogeneity, limited reproducibility, insufficient external validation and uncertainty regarding clinical utility continue to constrain translation. This Review critically synthesizes EEG-derived measures spanning spectral activity, oscillatory coupling, functional connectivity and dynamic brain states, examining their relationships with motor, cognitive and neuropsychiatric manifestations of PD. By distinguishing mechanistic interpretations, clinical associations and current levels of biomarker validation, it identifies opportunities and requirements for translating EEG-derived measures into reliable tools for individualized assessment and clinical decision-making.

articles_hidden.title: Enduring or Adaptable? A formal model and meta-analytic test of the stability of personality disorders
articles_hidden.authors: Orestis Zavlis; Michael Moutoussis; Peter Fonagy; Patrick Luyten
articles_hidden.abstract: Personality disorders have been traditionally framed as enduring dispositional conditions. Yet accumulating evidence suggests that they also reflect dynamic patterns of contextual adaptation. In this paper, we develop a formal framework that partitions personality stability into two components: an enduring portion (which is retained perfectly over time) and an adaptable portion (which dissipates over time, at either a fast or slow rate). After validating the model in computer simulations, we conduct a meta-analysis of 12 longitudinal investigations (N=17,785), yielding 145 test-retest correlations that quantify the stability of all personality conditions over 18 years. We then apply our formal model on these meta-analytic stability estimates to quantify the extent to which personality disorders are enduring vs. adaptable over time. Results indicate that most of personality pathology (60-70%) is adaptable over 18 years’ time, though it dissipates at a moderate rate (R≈55%). We conclude by suggesting that there is no formal distinction between personality pathology and psychopathology and outline a program aimed at studying all mental disorders as personality disorders.

articles_hidden.title: Large-scale analysis of the Galton-Crovitz cue-word technique shows strong word-specific retrieval biases in autobiographical memory
articles_hidden.authors: Steve M. J. Janssen; Jaap M. J. Murre
articles_hidden.abstract: With the Galton-Crovitz cueing technique, each participant reports personal events that are elicited by cue words, and then later dates these autobiographical memories. A persistent finding is a predominance of memories from the period in which the participants were between the ages of 10 and 30 years, which is called the ‘reminiscence bump’. Using the Internet, we collected nearly 140,000 memories with 64 cue words and plotted the lifetime distribution of each individual cue word. Many presumably neutral words, like chair, flower or sugar, most frequently triggered memories from early childhood (4 to 10 years), whereas others, such as wine, baby or army, triggered mostly memories from later ages. The selection of cue words—even seemingly unbiased ones—strongly affects the shape and location of the reminiscence bump. On the basis of these results, we recommend that, when the Galton-Crovitz cueing technique is used, word-specific effects should always be taken into account.

articles_hidden.title: Checkmating Cognitive Aging?  A Pilot Study Examining the Relationship between Chess Play and Cognitive Functioning in Older Adults
articles_hidden.authors: Caton Tsao; Aman Sreshta; Kaileigh A. Byrne
articles_hidden.abstract:
Objectives: Engagement in cognitively stimulating activities may support cognitive functioning in older adulthood, yet the potential benefits of chess participation remain understudied. This pilot study explored differences in working memory and global cognitive functioning between older adult chess players and non-chess players, while accounting for demographic characteristics and social engagement.
Methods: Eighty-three older adults (46 chess players; 37 non-chess players) completed computerized assessments of working memory capacity using a shortened Operation Span task and global cognitive functioning using a battery assessing memory, language, orientation, and executive functioning. Participants also reported their chess experience and social engagement. Analyses of covariance examined differences in cognitive performance between chess players and non-chess players, adjusting for age, gender, education, and social engagement.
Results: Older adult chess players (M = 14.62, SD = 6.35) exhibited better working memory capacity than non-chess players (M = 13.08, SD = 6.04, p=.032) independent of demographics and social engagement, while social engagement was associated with broader cognitive functioning (r = .267, p = .030).
Conclusions: These preliminary findings suggest that chess participation is selectively associated with working memory capacity, whereas broader social engagement is associated with global cognitive functioning. This distinction highlights the importance of examining specific forms of cognitive and social enrichment when investigating healthy cognitive aging. Larger longitudinal and experimental studies are needed to determine whether chess participation contributes to maintaining working memory in later life.

articles_hidden.title: Desarrollo de la Escala FAGIMAS: Fuentes de la Actitud hacia la Guerra de las Islas Malvinas del Atlántico Sur
articles_hidden.authors: Alejandro César Cosentino
articles_hidden.abstract: Esta investigación desarrolló y validó la Escala FAGIMAS (Fuentes de la Actitud hacia la Guerra de las Islas Malvinas del Atlántico Sur) mediante un diseño de investigación mixta secuencial. La investigación abarcó tres estudios: desarrollo de ítems, desarrollo de la escala y validación. El Estudio 1 incluyó 553 participantes que brindaron respuestas textuales sobre la Guerra de Malvinas, analizadas mediante lexicometría para desarrollar los ítems iniciales. El Estudio 2, con 397 participantes, utilizó análisis factorial exploratorio y modelado de ecuaciones estructurales para refinar el modelo, resultando una escala de 12 ítems que mide tres factores: patriotismo bélico, indignación bélica e interés bélico. El Estudio 3, con 670 cadetes militares, confirmó la estructura de la escala y examinó sus relaciones con la actitud hacia la Guerra de Malvinas. El modelo refinado confirmó buenos índices de ajuste robusto (CFI = 0.975, SRMR = 0.042, RMSEA = 0.067), adecuada confiabilidad de constructo (CR ≥ 0.83), validez convergente (AVE ≥ 0.59) y discriminante (HTMT2 ≤ 0.81). Los tres factores demostraron relaciones predictivas con la actitud hacia la Guerra de Malvinas, siendo interés bélico el que mostró la relación positiva más fuerte, seguido por patriotismo bélico, mientras que la indignación bélica mostró una relación negativa. Además, los factores del modelo refinado demostraron una capacidad predictiva incremental por sobre las fortalezas del carácter para la actitud hacia la Guerra de Malvinas. La Escala FAGIMAS es una medida confiable y válida para evaluar las fuentes cognitivas, afectivas y comportamentales de las actitudes hacia la Guerra de Malvinas.

articles_hidden.title: Development and Validation of Team Functional Degrees of Freedom (TfDoF): An Eco-Physical Variable for Functional Collective Off-ball Movements in Football
articles_hidden.authors: Li Xiao; Daniel Carrilho; enrico serra; Nelson Caldeira; Rui J. Lopes; Duarte Araújo
articles_hidden.abstract: In football, limited research has considered both the processes underlying collective behavior and its functional outcomes, constraining its practical applicability. In this study, we developed and validated an eco-physical variable, Team Functional Degrees of Freedom (TfDoF), to quantify how off-ball players dynamically coordinate their movements with teammates, opponents, and the ball to afford functional passing opportunities for a team in football. TfDoF was developed through a “glocal” spatial framework integrating centroid dynamics, Voronoi diagrams, dynamic pitch zoning, and a rule-based degrees-of-freedom approach. Validation comprised two complementary stages. First, expert-based validation involved seven football experts who evaluated the computational framework and identified passing opportunities in 30 match clips at the instant of passing. TfDoF showed a very strong correlation with expert-perceived passing opportunities (r = .98, p < .001), while all content validity indices exceeded .86, providing preliminary evidence of its content and convergent validity. Second, performance-based validation examined the relationship between TfDoF and pass outcomes using synchronized tracking and event data from 35 Italian Serie A matches (20,531 passes). Among six machine learning algorithms, XGBoost achieved the best classification performance (AUC = 0.909). SHAP analysis identified TfDoF as the most influential predictor of pass success (FI = 1.453), providing evidence of its predictive validity. Notably, TfDoF’s contribution to pass success was non-linear, with the greatest marginal effect occurring between TfDoF values of 5 and 7. Finally, we proposed a multi-timescale analytical framework demonstrating how TfDoF can support tactical analysis and coaching practice.

articles_hidden.title: Group psilocybin in an integrative retreat setting enhances social connection: an observational case report
articles_hidden.authors: Dayne Rayford; Shivani Dayal; Kosu Boudreau; Dingle Spence; Marik Hazan; AZA Stephen Allsop
articles_hidden.abstract:
Background and aims
Psilocybin can induce profound alterations in perception, emotion and self-referential processing. These changes are often accompanied by increased feelings of interpersonal connection, found via both psychometric survey data and anecdotally collected qualitative data. Despite recent increases in psychedelic research and treatment, most clinical trials have been performed in individualized patient treatment paradigms. Few studies have examined the outcomes of psilocybin in group contexts, even though ceremonial and group-based usage is historically ecological and may uniquely enhance group dynamics and social bonding.
Methods
This case study investigated psychological and social outcomes among participants (n=14) of a group psilocybin ceremony conducted in an integrative retreat setting. Participants completed a series of psychometric surveys and performed a social behavioral task designed to measure social perceptions at baseline and again at two timepoints following the psilocybin ceremonies.
Results and conclusions
Our results indicate significant increases in perceived social connectedness on the Social Perception Assessment (SPA) and the Watts Connectedness Scale (WCS) as well as significant decreases in distress on the Subjective Units of Distress Scale (SUDS). These findings highlight the importance of studying group-based psychedelic administration and suggest that collective settings may generate synergistic social benefits not captured in individual therapeutic models.

articles_hidden.title: Relationship between physical activity and resilience to stressors in non-clinical samples of adolescents and young adults: A systematic review
articles_hidden.authors: Bertalan Polner; Nina van den Broek; Anna Tyborowska; Linda Visser; Jacqueline Vink; Jonas Wachner; Margarita Karakara; Imke Adams
articles_hidden.abstract: While the benefits of physical activity for physical and mental health are well-established, it is less clear whether it also boosts resilience, defined as preserved mental health after exposure to stressors. Resilience in adolescents and young adults is critical given the high prevalence and lasting impact of mental health problems that emerge during development. Despite increasing recognition of the importance of physical activity for resilience, a structured overview is missing. Therefore, a systematic review of the literature was conducted including records published until December 2025 in PsycInfo, PubMed, Embase and Web of Science. We included 90 intervention and longitudinal studies on physical activity, and resilience in adolescents and young adults (10- 25 years) without a diagnosed mental health problem. In general, controlled intervention studies (n=39) showed various physiological and psychological benefits of physical activity in youth exposed to adversity and stressors. Intervention studies without a control group (n=26) and longitudinal observational studies (n=25) yielded comparable results. These findings imply that physical activity may causally impact resilience in youth exposed to adversity and stressors. It should be noted, however, that more preregistered, well-powered studies are required to corroborate these conclusions before formulating clinical or policy recommendations.

articles_hidden.title: Does creative engagement spill over into risk-taking behavior?
articles_hidden.authors: Shenghui Xiaoyong; Zhuoqi Yin; Huimin Kong; KelongLu
articles_hidden.abstract: Creative engagement may shape not only the ideas people generate but also how they approach risk in subsequent decisions, yet this possibility remains underexplored. Across three studies, we examined this relationship and whether general self-efficacy or affective state accounts for the relationship. Study 1 (N = 228) used a cross-sectional survey and found that everyday creative ideation behavior was positively associated with overall and domain-specific risk-taking propensity. General self-efficacy did not mediate this association. Study 2 (N = 83) experimentally compared risk taking after creative drawing versus standard coloring using a binary lottery choice. Creative drawing increased affective dominance but did not significantly influence subsequent risk taking. Study 3 (N = 94) compared risk taking after creative writing versus standard typing using a six-level investment-choice task. Creative writing increased both risk taking and affective dominance, but the change in dominance did not mediate the effect on risk taking. These findings suggest that creative engagement can influence subsequent financial risk taking, although the effect may depend on the creative task and the sensitivity of the risk measure. Neither general self-efficacy nor affective dominance explained this relationship, highlighting the need to investigate alternative psychological mechanisms.

articles_hidden.title: Optimization, Validation, and Application of the Chinese Barcelona Musical Reward Questionnaire (C-BMRQ)
articles_hidden.authors: Jiang Xintong; Hua Shan; Qin He; Yi Du
articles_hidden.abstract: The present study optimized, validated, and refined the Chinese version of the Barcelona Music Reward Questionnaire (C-BMRQ) to address key limitations of the existing culturally adapted iteration. We aimed to deliver a psychometrically robust, culturally tailored tool for assessing music reward sensitivity—a core component of musical aesthetic experience and creative engagement—among Chinese populations. Two sequential validation studies were conducted: Study 1 completed preliminary optimization and validation with two Beijing samples (Ns = 387, 391); Study 2 comprehensively verified the scale’s psychometric properties using three independent nationwide datasets plus Study 1’s second‑round data (N = 1,650). Rather than developing a novel scale, we employed a rigorous culture-adaptive strategy to optimize the existing version, preserving its original 20-item, five-factor structure (Music Seeking, Sensorimotor, Emotion Regulation, Emotional Evocation, Social Reward) without item deletion. Validation results confirmed the optimized C-BMRQ exhibited a stable five-factor model, strong internal consistency and test-retest reliability, configural and metric measurement invariance across gender and musical-training groups, and satisfactory convergent validity. Notably, the 10th percentile corresponded to a C-BMRQ total score of 69 in the pooled sample, providing a sample-derived reference value for low music reward sensitivity in Chinese adults. This value is intended for research use and requires independent clinical validation before being interpreted diagnostically. The optimized C-BMRQ is a reliable, culturally resonant instrument for Chinese populations, suitable for investigating musical aesthetic experiences, creativity in musical engagement, and cross-cultural differences in music reward processing, with meaningful implications for aesthetic neuroscience, creative arts research, and clinical practice.

articles_hidden.title: Do breadth and dose indices of exercise adherence measure the same thing? It depends on how unrecorded sessions are coded
articles_hidden.authors: FERNANDO GIMENO MARCO; Estela Prad Lucas
articles_hidden.abstract: Adherence to prescribed exercise between supervised sessions is routinely quantified with composite indices built from weekly self-reports, yet whether two reasonably constructed indices agree or diverge can hinge on decisions that are rarely scrutinized. Using weekly records from a community-based chronic-pain exercise program (14 participants, 173 person-weeks), we compared a breadth index (how many prescribed components were performed) with two frequency-based dose indices (uncapped and capped). Between persons, the indices ranked participants almost identically; within persons, however, their agreement proved highly sensitive to a single, usually invisible coding decision—whether components marked as performed but left unquantified are read as zero days. Naive zero-coding implied that breadth and dose capture different things within persons (correlations near .25), whereas activity-compatible scenarios moved these correlations to .41–.76. Rather than defend one imputation, we recommend reporting a bounded sensitivity analysis that brackets the plausible range, and we translate the findings into concrete guidance for designing exercise diaries and tracking apps so that participation and dose are recorded unambiguously.

articles_hidden.title: Using Language Models to Predict Values, Personality, Well-Being, and Meaning in Life From Ideal-Life Descriptions
articles_hidden.authors: Joffrey Fuhrer; Théo Desbordes
articles_hidden.abstract: Does the way we picture our ideal life reveal what we value, who we are, and how we thrive? In a preregistered study (N = 273), we tested whether free-form descriptions (median 109 words) and seven-keyword lists of one's ideal life predict a broad battery of psychological constructs: the Big Five, the ten Schwartz values, social dominance, political orientation, meaning in life, and subjective well-being. Using regularized linear probes on embeddings from transformer large language models (LLMs), inspired by model-interpretability research, we find that ideal-life narratives predict most constructs above chance in both conditions (mean r = 0.24 for free-form, mean r = 0.12 for keywords). This free-form advantage was concentrated on constructs people rarely name outright, such as achievement, benevolence, conformity, and emotional stability, implying that part of the signal lies in the manner of the telling rather than in the referents alone. Nineteen of the 24 constructs were recovered from roughly 120 words of text, a far broader battery than earlier language-based work, which has relied on much longer samples and focused on personality and well-being. Our approach offers an open, privacy-preserving alternative to zero-shot commercial LLMs, with comparable accuracy, no API cost, and freely released data and code.

articles_hidden.title: Supporting creativity education in the age of AI: The role of perceived exemplar source
articles_hidden.authors: Shenghui Xiaoyong; Yingning Lu; Yihui Liu; Yueyue Ge; Qiannan Ruan; Ke Jiang; KelongLu
articles_hidden.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI)-generated creative exemplars are increasingly used as scalable digital instructional resources in creativity education. However, it remains unclear whether labeling identical exemplars as human- or AI-generated shapes how learners engage in group creative activities. We tested this possibility in 113 dyads using an fNIRS hyperscanning group creative ideation paradigm. Dyads completed creative ideation tasks before, during, and after exemplar-stimulation. During stimulation, the human- and AI-attribution groups received identical exemplars labeled as produced by human or AI, whereas the control group received no exemplar. Human attribution increased idea uniqueness during stimulation relative to both the other phases and the AI-attribution and control groups. AI attribution temporarily increased switching among ideation pathways. Neither behavioral effect persisted after exemplar withdrawal. The two attribution groups did not differ in exemplar-category overlap or nearest-exemplar semantic distance, but human-attribution dyads rated the exemplars as more helpful. Human attribution also increased interbrain synchronization (IBS) in bilateral premotor and supplementary motor cortices during stimulation, whereas AI attribution was associated with decreased IBS in the left supramarginal gyrus and right frontopolar cortex from pre- to post-stimulation. Thus, exemplar-source attribution shapes the process and outcome of group creative ideation, revealing an important social-contextual factor in AI-supported creativity education.

articles_hidden.title: Beyond Color: A Constructivist Account of Chromatic Stimuli as Multidimensional Physiological and Psychological Events
articles_hidden.authors: David Henry Peterzell
articles_hidden.abstract: Color science has spent most of its history explaining one thing: the conscious sensation of hue, saturation, and brightness. Yet beside that success sits a growing list of inconvenient findings. Examples include ambiguous colors (one photograph seen as white-and-gold by some and blue-and-black by others); memory colors (a gray banana that looks faintly yellow); color before form (newly sighted patients who see color before objects); imagined or dreamed colors (chromatic experiences generated without light or eyes); aphantasia (people who cannot summon a color in imagination); synesthesia (a printed letter flooded with color); and large, stable individual differences in the colors people report. These are not marginal curiosities or isolated anomalies. They are the ordinary output of a system that the percept-centered framework leaves out. A chromatic stimulus does not simply produce a color percept; it initiates a broad physiological and psychological event, of which the percept is only one part. That percept is constructed at the moment of seeing by memory, language, attention, affect, and culture, and it shapes them in turn, a reciprocal determinism of percept and event. I develop this framework at three levels, as two nested theories: a new theory of color contained within a constructivist model of the entire chromatic event. The account retains trichromatic and some opponent-process theory rather than replacing them, but extends them by predicting phenomena the traditional framework treats as noise. Chief among these are the individual differences that, on this view, become the primary evidence for how color is constructed.

articles_hidden.title: General and domain-specific genetic signals shape educational outcomes in children and adults
articles_hidden.authors: Alexandra Starr; René Pool; Hailey Adelene Davis; Iorana Fosca Alice Fey; Ana Luisa Henriques Fürst; Eugenia Kis; Yola Sol; Lannie Ligthart; Bruno Sauce; Elsje van Bergen
articles_hidden.abstract:
Abstract
Purpose: Individual differences in literacy and numeracy – that is, how well one can read, write, and work with numbers – emerge early in childhood and are crucial indicators of later educational success. Twin and family studies revealed substantial heritability of literacy and numeracy, and genetic overlap between these domains. Yet, it is unclear whether measured genomic variation shows a similarly overlapping or domain-specific pattern, and whether such molecular signals also predict adults’ educational attainment.
Method: In N=15,669 participants (52.7% female; Netherlands Twin Register), we predicted children’s literacy, numeracy, and academic achievement, and adults’ educational attainment from genetic predispositions. Children’s learning outcomes were assessed via teacher and parent reports and a nationwide test (age M=12.25 years). Adults reported their highest educational qualification (age M= 42.47 years). We derived polygenic scores (PGSs) for years of education, dyslexia, and reading skills to predict these outcomes. 
Results: All three PGSs significantly predicted educational outcomes, but the broad years-of-education PGS exceeded the domain-specific dyslexia and reading-skills PGSs. The years-of-education PGS explained up to 10.7% in children’s academic achievement and 13.2% in adults’ attainment, suggesting that broader, large-scale PGS of general education capture much of the genetic signal shared across learning domains.
Conclusion: Findings indicate both shared and specific genetic influences on learning. Broad, high-power PGSs maximise prediction, whereas literacy-focused PGSs highlight domain-specific signal. While current PGSs are not suitable for individual prediction, they are valuable for accounting for genetic propensities and improving causal inference in developmental and education research.

articles_hidden.title: Statistical Learning of Distractor Suppression Generalizes Across Contexts Despite Blocked Learning
articles_hidden.authors: Milan Geldhof; Brent Vernaillen; Christophe Vanhouwe; Louisa Bogaerts
articles_hidden.abstract: Statistical learning can shape visual attention by enabling spatial suppression of locations that frequently contain distractors. Although learned suppression may be context-dependent, the underlying factors driving this dependency remain unclear. While previous research has largely focused on the nature of the context itself, less attention has been paid to how context–regularity pairs are presented, particularly whether they are blocked or intermixed across trials. Multiple uninterrupted pairings may be necessary for less salient contextual cues, such as background colors or images, to support context-dependent learning. The present preregistered, high- powered study (N = 136) therefore used a blocked presentation, with two blocks each pairing a unique background color with a high-frequency distractor location, followed by an intermixed testing phase with equiprobable distractor locations. Results show that although distractors reliably captured attention, the background context did not affect response times in the testing block, with Bayesian analyses providing decisive evidence for context-independent suppression. These results show that implicitly learned distractor suppression is highly robust, persistent, and generalizes across non-task- relevant contexts, even when context–regularity associations are repeated and uninterrupted during learning.

articles_hidden.title: Color cues, developmental coupling, and the limits of the late-sighted model: A commentary on Vogelsang et al. (2024)
articles_hidden.authors: David Henry Peterzell
articles_hidden.abstract:
Vogelsang et al. (2024) report in Science that congenitally blind individuals who gain sight late in life rely disproportionately on color cues for object recognition, unlike normally sighted controls. They propose that this pattern reflects the adaptive value of neonatal color immaturity: because typical infants experience a period of degraded chromatic input, they develop object representations grounded in luminance rather than color.
The theoretical account, however, rests on an incomplete engagement with the developmental literature. Decades of research indicate that color and luminance sensitivity are developmentally coupled through shared photoreceptor immaturity: the same front-end bottleneck that degrades chromatic input in neonates simultaneously degrades luminance and spatial processing. If this coupling is real, there is no luminance-first window, because the bottleneck lifts for both dimensions together. The account's central premise is therefore undermined not by arguing independence, but by showing that color and luminance do not develop in the sequence the account requires.
I further identify methodological concerns: a small and unusual sample, a fixed order confound in the primary behavioral task, a computational model implementing a binary switch rather than the gradual chromatic cascade of normal development, and a color sensitivity test using non-equiluminant stimuli, leaving open the possibility that luminance rather than chromatic contrast sensitivity drove performance.
Together, these issues require qualification of the conclusions of Vogelsang et al. and reconciliation of the proposed account with classical findings in infant visual development. This broader question remains important, but the answer is unlikely to hinge on color alone.

articles_hidden.title: Registered Reports as the default pathway for confirmatory publication
articles_hidden.authors: Marta Topor; Joshua Silberstein Bamford; Marina Bazhydai; Zhang Chen; Hu Chuan-Peng; Clare Conry-Murray; Thiago Leiros Costa; Antica Culina; Mario Dalmaso; Zoltan Dienes
articles_hidden.abstract: By rewarding speed, volume, and coherent positive narratives, traditional publishing incentivizes questionable scientific practices and analytic flexibility. The latter especially contributes to blurring the distinction between exploration and confirmation, which inflates the apparent strength of confirmatory claims. This systemic issue has gone unchecked for decades, leaving the scientific community with a body of scholarly literature that is unreliable and lacking validity. Registered Reports (RRs) address problematic publishing practices by requiring a priori registration of confirmatory tests, which is peer-reviewed before the research begins (stage 1). The editorial acceptance of a stage 1 plan establishes a commitment to publication regardless of research outcomes. Publication remains, nonetheless, contingent on a second peer review and editorial scrutiny (stage 2) to verify that the approved plan was followed, all deviations were transparently disclosed and justified, confirmatory and exploratory claims are clearly delineated, and the integrity of the design was maintained. Meta-scientific comparisons indicate that RRs reduce outcome-based publication bias and improve methodological rigor without compromising perceived novelty. By making accepted RR protocols and their review history citable research outputs, RRs also strengthen recognition for peer-review work. In this perspective, we argue that RRs should become the primary mode of confirmatory publication moving forward.

articles_hidden.title: On Color and Emotion: What Can Vision Science Learn from the Rorschach?
articles_hidden.authors: David Henry Peterzell
articles_hidden.abstract: For a century, clinicians have recorded how people use color when they interpret inkblots, rank colored cards, or draw. They believed that how a person handles color reveals how that person handles feeling. Vision science has rarely read this literature, and the most complete modern review of color and emotion research excluded it. This paper introduces the projective color literature to vision scientists in plain language. Three conclusions follow. First, the tradition’s central belief, that chromatic color stirs emotion directly, was tested from the 1940s onward and largely failed. Second, narrower findings survived. The degree to which a person lets color lead over form in an ambiguous image is modestly related to several independently assessed clinical, behavioral, and biological outcomes. Some indices that set color in balance with other responses, such as coping versus overload, are also supported. What these scores measure is disputed. Third, the findings concern how color is weighted against form, which vision science already studies, yet only one study has linked that weighting to an object-recognition task, and none has used calibrated stimuli. I then read both literatures through a constructivist model of color in which the percept and the wider event it belongs to determine each other reciprocally. On this reading, the question is not only whether color influences emotion but also whether emotion influences color. The projective tradition raised the second question. Modern color-emotion science has mostly set it aside. Five studies are proposed that would join the two fields.

articles_hidden.title: Artificial observers and real individual differences: A roadmap for a computational psychometrics of vision
articles_hidden.authors: David Henry Peterzell
