articles_hidden.abstract: Deep neural networks are increasingly used as models of vision, yet they are evaluated against the average observer: average performance, average neural response, average representational geometry. This discards one of the richest constraints on theory: stable individual differences. Fitting the average is necessary but not sufficient. I argue that future models should be judged not only by their fit to mean human performance, but by whether populations of artificial observers reproduce the covariance structure and latent factors found across human observers. Two mature but disconnected literatures motivate this. Decades of factor-analytic psychophysics and electrophysiology show that interindividual variation is signal, not noise: the pattern of correlations among observers reveals the number and tuning of underlying mechanisms, and fractionates vision into many narrow factors rather than one general ability. Meanwhile, neural networks differing only in random initialization develop measurably different internal representations, so any single trained network is one sample from a distribution of possible observers. Joining these yields a computational psychometrics of vision: construct a designed population of artificial observers (varying in architecture, initialization, training diet, and front-end sampling), submit them to the same latent-variable analyses used on humans, and test whether the recovered factor structure matches. Recent work showing that seed-varied networks align with specific individuals is an existence proof. This article generalizes it into a framework, a staged roadmap, and a benchmark, together with the safeguards that keep such a benchmark from becoming an optimization target, for testing hypotheses about human visual variation with artificial observer populations.

articles_hidden.title: Latent visual mechanisms as computational phenotypes: Toward a precision science of vision
articles_hidden.authors: David Henry Peterzell
articles_hidden.abstract: Vision science has traditionally sought mechanisms shared across observers, treating individual differences as noise. Yet factor-analytic and latent-variable studies show that variation among observers is highly structured, recovering reproducible dimensions in contrast sensitivity, color, stereopsis, motion, and face recognition, among others. What are these latent dimensions? I propose they be treated as candidate computational phenotypes: a term borrowed from computational psychiatry and re-operationalized for vision as a stable, measurable pattern of visual information processing recovered from the covariance structure of individual differences. A computational phenotype is not a latent factor, mechanism, endophenotype, or biomarker; it occupies Marr's algorithmic level, between behavior and biology, and earns the name only by meeting stringent criteria of reliability, replication, convergent validity, and mechanistic relevance. I review candidate phenotypes drawn from many laboratories, recast development, aging, and disease as perturbations of phenotypic structure, and turn the strongest objection (that vision has no common factor) into support, since the relevant phenotypes are narrow and mechanism-specific. The payoff spans audiences: diagnostic profiles for clinicians, a non-invasive way to count and test visual mechanisms for basic scientists, and performance-predicting traits for human-factors work. The framework moves vision science from the average observer toward a precision science of visual computation.

articles_hidden.title: A Brief Intervention Highlighting Counter-stereotypical Role Models Changes Children’s  Gender Stereotypes about Values and Careers
articles_hidden.authors: Katharina Block; Sophie Arnold; Heather MacRae; Andrei Cimpian
articles_hidden.abstract:
Care-oriented values and careers are vital, yet men remain less engaged with them. We tested a
brief, preregistered role-model intervention to reduce children’s gender stereotypes about
communion (caring for others) and agency (achievement and independence). We also examined
whether this intervention would narrow gender differences in children’s own values and career
interests. Seven- to 10-year-olds from the US and Canada (N = 244; 121 boys, 123 girls) viewed
six animated vignettes about fictional children who grew up to choose careers aligned with their
values. In the “stereotypical” condition, girls were communal and entered communal careers,
while boys were agentic and entered agentic careers. In the “counter-stereotypical” condition,
these pairings were reversed. A third, “counter-stereotypical + status” condition added wealth
cues to both careers. Compared with the stereotypical condition, both counter-stereotypical
conditions weakened children’s gender stereotypes about communal and agentic values and
careers. They also reduced gender differences in children’s own communal values and career
interests, although these effects were smaller and less consistent. Wealth cues did not strengthen
the intervention. These findings suggest that counter-stereotypical role models are a promising,
scalable method for combating stereotypes that steer boys away from communion—though
likely one component of broader efforts.

articles_hidden.title: Choosing Stimuli Wisely by Using Individual Differences: A Step-by-Step Tutorial for the One-Stimulus-Per-Factor Principle in Vision Science and Optometric Assessment
articles_hidden.authors: David Henry Peterzell
articles_hidden.abstract: Given that data collection time in vision research and clinical assessment is limited, investigators and clinicians must select stimuli that maximize diagnostic information with minimum redundancy. This article proposes that analyzing individual differences—through factor analysis (FA), principal component analysis (PCA), and multidimensional scaling (MDS)—offers a principled approach. The covariance structure of individual variation reveals the minimum number of independent factors underlying a visual function, and therefore the minimum number of stimuli needed for efficient, non-redundant characterization. I term this the One-Stimulus-Per-Factor Principle: one well-chosen stimulus per factor is both necessary and sufficient. A complementary rule governs discovery: at least two to three stimuli per expected factor are needed to establish the factor structure. Converging evidence from luminance and chromatic contrast sensitivity, stereoscopic disparity, motion, hue scaling, face recognition, perceptual organization, and other domains shows that the dimensionality of individual variation is often lower than dense sampling suggests—and sometimes higher than sparse clinical testing captures. The approach also tests construct validity, revealing whether behavioral measures index the mechanisms investigators assume. These findings carry implications for clinical instruments across contrast sensitivity, color vision, stereopsis, and visual field assessment, many of which either oversample a single factor or undersample the full factor space. The same framework clarifies psychiatric applications—including contrast-sensitivity changes in depression, schizophrenia, and ADHD—by separating retinal-neural deficits from optical contributions such as higher-order aberrations and from attentional lapses, and it extends to oculomotor biomarkers. The article develops the Principle as a step-by-step tutorial, with a worked example.

articles_hidden.title: Comparative Optimism for Getting Infected With COVID-19: An Individual Participant Data Meta-Analysis and Critical Reflection on Research Practices
articles_hidden.authors: Lars König; Frank Renkewitz
articles_hidden.abstract: Comparative optimism (believing one’s own risk is lower than others’) has been widely studied. Nonetheless, important methodological features have largely remained unrecognized. Focusing on a single event (contracting COVID-19), we estimated the average effect, tested moderators with attention to measurement artifacts, and appraised methodological quality. We synthesized 135 effect sizes from 50 studies (38 articles; sample sizes summing to 88,935, not necessarily unique participants) using a multilevel model with random effects for study, article, and nationality. We then examined moderators at both aggregated and individual-participant levels. Although, on average, comparative optimism was observed (d = 0.334, 95% CI [0.225, 0.444]), true effects varied substantially, and the meta-analytic prediction interval ranged from −0.371 to 1.040. Strikingly, this substantial heterogeneity was observed despite our efforts to control for various potential sources of heterogeneity during data collection. Measurement format was the most consistent moderator, with indirect assessments yielding larger adjusted effects than direct assessments, whereas longer response scales were not consistently associated with smaller effects. Effects were larger in samples collected in 2021 than in 2020, but this exploratory finding was sensitive to one article. The association with national collectivism was unclear in the primary model. Individual-participant analyses showed no clear overall associations for age, gender, or education. Response distributions indicated that nearly half of participants reported lower personal risk than others, more than one third reported equal risk, and about one sixth reported higher risk. Small-study and selection-model analyses suggested possible selective reporting. In sum, although we observed an average comparative optimism effect for contracting COVID-19, the generalizability of the effect and its measured correlates is limited by substantial heterogeneity and the influence of measurement choices and study context.

articles_hidden.title: Investigating the Factors Motivating the Adoption of Optimal Attentional Strategies
articles_hidden.authors: Tianyu Zhang; Molly R McKinney; Isaac Savelson; Jessica Irons; Andrew B. Leber
articles_hidden.abstract: Our goal-directed attentional control abilities enable us to flexibly maximize how efficiently we search the visual environment.  However, a growing body of research reveals that we often fail to use these abilities.  Here, we question how motivational incentives might be used to improve attentional control strategies.  Using the Adaptive Choice Visual Search (Irons & Leber, 2018), a task designed to measure attentional strategy use, we manipulated motivation in two ways.  In Experiment 1, we limited the exposure of the visual search items, and in Experiment 2, we provided a greater monetary reward for faster search performance.  In both experiments, we reasoned that participants would choose the search strategies that enabled faster target identification times; faster search would reduce errors in Experiment 1 and increase earnings in Experiment 2.  Results showed that the time-pressure manipulation failed to induce more optimal strategy choices, while the performance-contingent reward manipulation did induce a modest improvement in strategy.  Overall, we find some evidence of a link between motivation and strategy optimization, although methods to elicit a more robust boost in optimization remain elusive.  Further work is needed in this understudied but vital domain of research.

articles_hidden.title: The Psychology of GLP-1 Receptor Agonists: Evidence for Distinct Effects on Reward, Interoception and Cognition
articles_hidden.authors: Poppy Watson; Simone Rehn; Mike Kendig; Dominic M. D. Tran; Justin Mahlberg; Kristi Griffiths
articles_hidden.abstract: Glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1 RAs) are widely used for obesity and type 2 diabetes, supporting weight loss and glycaemic control through effects on appetite and ingestive behaviour. The psychobiological mechanisms underlying these effects remain unclear. We reviewed evidence for candidate mechanisms and analysed quantitative and qualitative self-reported changes in appetite-related experiences from 704 people using GLP-1 RAs. Participants reported multiple changes that appeared distinct for food versus alcohol, with reductions in food urges and cravings largely independent of changes in alcohol use. Enhanced awareness and utilisation of hunger and satiety signals were frequently described, suggesting potential changes in interoceptive processes. Changes in enjoyment of eating were largely independent of reductions in food cravings, urges to eat, and gastrointestinal side effects. Improved ability to eat in a goal-directed manner was also frequently reported. Results support the presence of multiple cognitive and behavioural processes contributing to reduced food intake and provide testable hypotheses to explore in experimental work designed to isolate effects of GLP-1 RAs on goal-directed control, interoceptive awareness, attention, memory, and executive function.

articles_hidden.title: Group psilocybin in an integrative retreat setting enhances social connection: an observational case report
articles_hidden.authors: Dayne Rayford; Shivani Dayal; Kosu Boudreau; Dingle Spence; Marik Hazan; AZA Stephen Allsop
articles_hidden.abstract:
Background and aims
Psilocybin can induce profound alterations in perception, emotion and self-referential processing. These changes are often accompanied by increased feelings of interpersonal connection, found via both psychometric survey data and anecdotally collected qualitative data. Despite recent increases in psychedelic research and treatment, most clinical trials have been performed in individualized patient treatment paradigms. Few studies have examined the outcomes of psilocybin in group contexts, even though ceremonial and group-based usage is historically ecological and may uniquely enhance group dynamics and social bonding.
Methods
This case study investigated psychological and social outcomes among participants (n=14) of a group psilocybin ceremony conducted in an integrative retreat setting. Participants completed a series of psychometric surveys and performed a social behavioral task designed to measure social perceptions at baseline and again at two timepoints following the psilocybin ceremonies.
Results and conclusions
Our results indicate significant increases in perceived social connectedness on the Social Perception Assessment (SPA) and the Watts Connectedness Scale (WCS) as well as significant decreases in distress on the Subjective Units of Distress Scale (SUDS). These findings highlight the importance of studying group-based psychedelic administration and suggest that collective settings may generate synergistic social benefits not captured in individual therapeutic models.

articles_hidden.title: LOVE AND CHANGE
articles_hidden.authors: Elzė Sigutė Mikalonytė; Julian Savulescu; Brian D. Earp
articles_hidden.abstract: Philosophers and laypeople often have two seemingly conflicting intuitions: that love must be caused by who the beloved is and that it should persist despite personal change. Little attention has been paid to which changes are, and which are not, compatible with the requirement that real love should persist – and associated obligations. Across three online studies with UK-based participants (total N = 2482), we used vignettes in which a person’s moral character, memory, or physical appearance changed. We found that judgments on whether love that ended after the change was real and whether people should remain bound by their marital obligations depend on the same properties as judgments about the continuity of personal identity. For both the continuity of personal identity and love, together with the obligations that love brings, moral properties were the most important, followed by memory, while physical properties were considered considerably less important. Negative changes in moral character or autobiographical memory, compared to positive changes, were seen as more disruptive both to identity and marital obligations, and more compatible with past love being real.

articles_hidden.title: Feasibility and engagement of smartphone delivered yoga imagery with or without personalized avatars in residential substance use treatment: The AT-REACH nonrandomized pilot
articles_hidden.authors: Dennis McChargue; Byrav Ramamurthy; Wenyue Wang; Ashlin Ondrusek; Srikar Chanamolu; anna henson
articles_hidden.abstract: Background. Brief guided imagery may provide a practical way to rehearse a yoga experience between live sessions. We evaluated smartphone delivery and repeated use of yoga imagery and explored whether adding a personalized animated avatar was associated with different outcomes. Methods. This nonrandomized pilot enrolled 35 adults in four cohorts at residential substance use recovery facilities in Nebraska. Participants received an introductory yoga session and brief app delivered imagery practices, with three daily prompts. Thirteen participants received imagery with an animated avatar and 22 received imagery without the avatar. Allocation was by seat choice rather than a randomized sequence; the fourth cohort received the comparison condition only. We summarized app use over the first 28 days of logs, rated emotion changes around practice, and baseline to exit questionnaire outcomes. Results. All 35 initiated the app and 27 (77%) completed the exit assessment. Participants logged 2901 sessions, a median of 86 per person (interquartile range 62 to 104). At least three sessions were logged on 59% of days and at least one on 68%. The between group engagement effect was close to zero but imprecise (Hedges g = 0.03, 95% CI -0.66 to 0.71). Mean negative emotion intensity changed by -8.9 points on a 0 to 100 scale (95% CI -15.9 to -1.9). The baseline adjusted DERS total difference was 9.2 points (95% CI -6.7 to 25.2). The exploratory DERS Awareness change effect favored animated visual support (g = 0.89, 95% CI 0.06 to 1.73), but the cohort adjusted exit difference was smaller and imprecise (-1.30 points, 95% CI -5.05 to 2.46). Other questionnaire findings were mixed. Conclusions. The pilot documents repeated use of brief guided yoga imagery in residential recovery settings. It does not establish imagery efficacy, equivalence between formats, or an added benefit of animated visual support. Randomized evaluation with consistent assessment and complete delivery logs is warranted.

articles_hidden.title: Poor reliability in measuring habituation: Implications for clinical and translational research on exposure and extinction
articles_hidden.authors: Emma Dear; Gabrielle Rose Messner; Julia Levitan; Richie Ward Gray; Cheri A Levinson; Eric Lenze; Jaclyn Weisman; Thomas Rodebaugh
articles_hidden.abstract:
Objective: The purpose of this study was to investigate the reliability of change indices in exposure therapy. 
Method: We analyzed data from 119 adults with elevated social anxiety who participated in studies of public speaking exposures. Participants reported their distress using the Subjective Units of Distress Scale (SUDS) at regular intervals. The reliability of within-session habituation, between-session habituation, and expectancy change measures were estimated. 
Results: Commonly used measures of between-session habituation (BSH) typically demonstrated only moderate reliability, and commonly used measures of within-session habituation (WSH) typically demonstrated poor reliability. Exploratory tests in expectancy change indices suggests these findings apply to other measures of change during exposure.  
Conclusions: Our results indicate that measures underlying the study of habituation may be inadequate because of low reliability. This threatens the foundation of clinical and translational research, such that no substantive conclusions can be drawn from them.

articles_hidden.title: Reward Contingency Shapes Incidental Reward Effects on Cognitive Flexibility
articles_hidden.authors: Joseph M Orr; Beatrice Lomeo; Juan Balcazar; Daniela Porro
articles_hidden.abstract: Voluntary task switching (VTS) provides a useful paradigm for examining how recent reward outcomes are associated with the balance between cognitive stability and flexibility. We investigated whether reward-history effects on task choice varied as a function of cue–outcome contingency. Participants (N = 616) completed a VTS task with performance-contingent rewards. Reward contingency was manipulated between-subjects at probabilities of100\%, 80\%, 70\%, and 60\%. Switch probability was modeled using logistic mixed-effects regression. The relationship between prior reward outcomes and the current reward prospect in predicting switch behavior differed across probability conditions. Reward transition effects were larger at 100\% and 80\% than at 70\% and 60\%. Secondary analyses further indicated that outcomes that were unexpected given the cue–reward mapping were associated with subsequent switching in some comparisons, although evidence that these associations systematically varied with probability was mixed. Because task choices did not influence reward outcomes, the observed effects are more consistent with carry-over associations between reward history and task selection than with reward-guided exploration or reward maximization. Exploratory individual-differences analyses suggested that reward transition effects were more pronounced in males than in females; additionally, trait-level reward sensitivity moderated the magnitude of reward transition effects on switch behavior. Overall, the findings are consistent with the hypothesis that cue-outcome contingency modulates the extent to which recent rewards are followed by particular task-choice patterns, although further research is required to clarify the mechanisms through which reward uncertainty may contribute to these effects.

articles_hidden.title: Beyond Initial Crisis Recognition: Suicide-Risk Responses of ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini Across 14-Turn Ukrainian-Language Conversations
articles_hidden.authors: Hryhorii Kuzyk; Oleg Salamon; Liliia Andreieva; Kateryna Drozdova
articles_hidden.abstract: Nine deployed conversational systems mostly recognised the crisis, but it disappeared from their behaviour once the conversation moved on. We ran 16 scenarios in ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini as 14-message conversations (48 dialogues): crisis signals alternated with distraction, turn 13 introduced a new person at risk, and turn 14 was sent a day later. Coding was binary, as in the previous study, with clinical verification; two crisis-contour specifications were tested separately. New crisis signals drew a reaction in 87, 95, and 76 of 96 responses, respectively; the crisis stopped being mentioned mainly at an everyday message. The new person at risk drew a reaction in 44 of 48 responses; after a day, 29 retained crisis content. All 14 turns drew a 'yes' code in 4, 7, and 0 of 16 conversations. Reacting to the new person did not guarantee correct allocation of roles and actions. Both contour specifications produced safety-relevant errors. Neither hypothesis was supported: the systems behaved differently, and the same rule, introduced as a single package, did not stabilise their behaviour. Recognition, retention, and reconfiguration at a transition are distinct properties; the weakest is retention of the prior state and tracking of each person's trajectory.

articles_hidden.title: A clinician-informed framework for precision psychotherapy in psychosis
articles_hidden.authors: No authors listed
articles_hidden.abstract: Background. Despite evidence supporting cognitive behavioural therapy for psychosis (CBTp), engagement and treatment response remain highly variable, and robust predictors are lacking. Existing research may overlook clinically relevant factors. We aimed to identify candidate predictors of CBTp engagement and outcomes by integrating clinicians’ perspectives with the existing literature. Methods. Twenty clinical psychologists experienced in delivering CBTp participated in semi-structured interviews. Using a mixed-methods design, we first identified candidate predictors through inductive framework analysis of unprompted accounts. Clinicians subsequently rated the perceived importance of these and 32 literature-derived factors on a 10-point scale. Mean ratings and variability were examined to characterise clinician agreement. Findings were integrated into a candidate predictor framework linked to available measurement instruments. Results. Clinicians spontaneously identified 38 factors, of which 16 were absent from the literature-derived list. Frequently identified factors included readiness and motivation (90%), cognitive flexibility (85%), social support (80%), previous experiences of care and therapy (70%), and socioeconomic and environmental stability (70%). Clinicians emphasised therapy-related, contextual, and clinical management factors, including expectations of therapy, substance misuse, and medication, which remain underrepresented in prediction research. Literature-derived factors receiving relatively high importance ratings and agreement included insight, cognitive flexibility, hopelessness, and social functioning. Demographic characteristics were generally considered less important. Conclusion. Clinicians identified factors extending beyond those conventionally investigated as predictors of CBTp engagement and outcomes. The resulting clinician-informed measurement framework provides a broader, clinically grounded candidate predictor set to guide prospective studies and the development of personalised prediction models in psychosis. Keywords: Precision psychotherapy, psychological intervention, CBT, psychosis, schizophrenia
